lessons.title: Edward's Inheritance: From Henry III to a New King
lessons.description: Edward I’s accession in 1272, Henry III’s troubled legacy and the problems facing the new king.
lessons.content_html:
A King Crowned in Absence

When Henry III died on 16 November 1272, his son Edward was thousands of miles away on crusade. Edward did not rush home. He was already recognised as king from the day his father died — the first English ruler to be treated as king before any coronation — and the realm was governed by a council of trusted men until he reached London almost two years later. He was finally crowned at Westminster Abbey on 19 August 1274. The kingdom Edward inherited was not the orderly realm a strong medieval king needed. It was a country still bruised from civil war, where great magnates had grown used to challenging royal authority and where ordinary people had lost faith in royal justice.

Key Fact

Edward I became king on 16 November 1272 but was not crowned until 19 August 1274. He was on crusade when his father Henry III died and travelled home slowly through France and Gascony, confident that no one would challenge his right to rule.

Henry III’s Damaged Crown

Henry III had ruled for fifty-six years — the longest reign of any medieval English king — but his rule had been weak. He spent vast sums on foreign schemes, especially a doomed plan to put his second son Edmund on the throne of Sicily, and relied on unpopular foreign favourites at court. By the late 1250s the leading barons had had enough.

In 1258 a group of barons led by Simon de Montfort forced Henry to accept the Provisions of Oxford. These placed the king under the supervision of a council of fifteen barons, demanded regular parliaments, and reformed local government. For the first time, an English king was effectively put on a leash by his nobility. Henry quickly tried to wriggle free, getting the pope to release him from his oath in 1261.

When Henry rejected the Provisions, the kingdom slid into civil war. At the Battle of Lewes in 1264, Simon de Montfort captured both Henry III and the young Lord Edward, ruling England in the king’s name for over a year. In January 1265 Montfort summoned a parliament that included not only barons and bishops but also two knights from each shire and two burgesses from selected towns — a wider assembly than England had ever seen.

Edward escaped his guards in May 1265 and led the royalist counter-attack. At the Battle of Evesham on 4 August 1265, royalist forces trapped Montfort’s smaller army in a loop of the River Avon. Montfort was killed and his body hacked apart. Edward had won, but the war left England exhausted, scattered with armed bands of disinherited rebels and deeply suspicious of royal promises.

Edward the Crusader

After helping his father restore order through the Statute of Marlborough in 1267, Edward took the cross and left for the Holy Land in 1270. His crusade achieved little militarily but did a great deal for his reputation. He survived an assassination attempt by a Nizari Ismaili (sometimes called ‘Assassins’) at Acre in 1272 — a story retold across Christendom. By the time he returned home, Edward arrived not just as a king but as a famous warrior in his own right, with a reputation that quietened any thought of rebellion.

Problems Waiting for the New King

When Edward finally landed at Dover on 2 August 1274, the inheritance was difficult. Local government had drifted: sheriffs and other royal officers had taken bribes, seized land that did not belong to them, and let private courts swallow up royal jurisdiction. The royal income was too small for the king’s ambitions, partly because earlier kings had granted away crown lands. Disputes between the king and the great liberties of the magnates were unresolved. And in Wales, Llywelyn ap Gruffudd refused to attend the coronation or pay homage — an open challenge that would soon force a war.

Contemporaries called Edward ‘Longshanks’ because he was unusually tall — over six feet, with long arms suited to swordsmanship. He was disciplined, hard-working and deeply religious, but he could also be quick-tempered and merciless to anyone he thought had betrayed him. His marriage to Eleanor of Castile (married 1254) was famously close; she travelled with him on crusade and on campaign, and bore at least fourteen children.

Edward saw kingship as a duty to deliver justice and recover royal rights that earlier kings had let slip away. The chronicler Walter of Guisborough recorded the king’s personal motto: ‘Keep faith’. This combination of legal mind, military energy and confidence in his own authority shaped almost every act of his reign.

Relations with the Nobility

Unlike Henry III, Edward had grown up among the great barons and fought beside many of them at Evesham. He worked with leading magnates such as the earls of Gloucester and Norfolk rather than relying on foreign favourites. Yet he also intended to claw back rights and revenues the nobles had absorbed during the chaos. The Hundred Rolls inquiry, launched within months of his coronation, would put that intention on paper. From the very start, Edward’s reign would be a balancing act — respecting the nobility enough to keep their support, while pressing hard on their privileges.

Key Fact

The problems waiting for Edward in 1274 included corrupt local officials, a shrunken royal income, magnates holding privileges that should have belonged to the crown, and an unanswered challenge from Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in Wales.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Effects’ question on this topic, link the events of Henry III’s reign directly to Edward’s actions as king. The strongest answers do not just describe the Provisions of Oxford or the Battle of Evesham — they explain how those events caused Edward to launch the Hundred Rolls, distrust over-mighty barons, and want a stronger crown. Use precise medieval terms (magnate, liberty, statute) and avoid vague phrases like ‘he made laws’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Edward I became king on 16 November 1272 while on crusade and was crowned on 19 August 1274; the realm was governed by a council in his absence.
  • Henry III’s reign produced the Provisions of Oxford (1258), Simon de Montfort’s parliament (1265) and the Battle of Evesham (1265), leaving Edward with a damaged crown.
  • In 1274 Edward inherited corrupt local government, weak royal finances, magnates holding lost royal rights, and an open challenge from Llywelyn of Wales.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Henry III’s reign on the kingdom that Edward I inherited in 1272.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Civil war between the king and his barons (1264–65) left England exhausted, with armed bands of ‘disinherited’ rebels still active when Edward came home; this meant Edward needed to restore order and secure the loyalty of the magnates from his very first days as king.
• The Provisions of Oxford (1258) and Simon de Montfort’s parliament (1265) had set a precedent that the great barons could supervise or even capture the king; Edward inherited a tradition of baronial assertion that pushed him to clarify and defend royal rights through inquiries and statutes.
• Henry III’s reliance on foreign favourites and expensive foreign schemes (the ‘Sicilian Business’) drained the treasury; this caused Edward to launch the Hundred Rolls inquiry in 1274–75 to find out what crown lands and revenues had been lost.
• Local government had become corrupt, with sheriffs and bailiffs taking bribes and private liberties expanding; this caused Edward to challenge baronial franchises through the Quo Warranto inquiries and to begin the long programme of legal reform.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking at least three effects of Henry III’s reign directly to Edward’s situation in 1272–74, using precise terminology.
Secure: Two clear effects developed with relevant detail and explicit links to Edward’s inheritance.
Developing: Some effects identified but explanation is partial or descriptive rather than causal.
Emerging: Simple statements about Henry III with no clear link to what Edward inherited.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the political settlement Edward I inherited in 1272.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A royal council ruled in Edward’s name while he completed his crusade and travelled home through France and Gascony — recognition of the king before coronation was a new precedent.
• The Provisions of Oxford (1258), although effectively dead, had established that great barons might claim a right to limit royal power through a council and regular parliaments.
• The crown lands and revenues had shrunk, leaving Edward with weak finances and a need to pursue inquiries such as the Hundred Rolls.
• Disputes with the Welsh prince Llywelyn ap Gruffudd were unresolved — he refused to attend the coronation or pay homage.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail. Two clearly separate features required for full marks.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Battle of Evesham (1265) for the reign of Edward I.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The battle restored royal authority decisively: Simon de Montfort was killed and his army destroyed, ending the threat of baronial rule and allowing Henry III — and later Edward — to govern as king again.
• Evesham gave the young Lord Edward a military reputation just as he was about to inherit the throne; he had escaped captivity and led the royalist counter-attack, which made him a credible warrior-king at home and on crusade.
• The defeat of Montfort’s reform movement meant Edward came to the throne in 1272 free of the Provisions of Oxford, but he never forgot how close the magnates had come to running the kingdom — this shaped his determination to recover royal rights through the Hundred Rolls and Quo Warranto.
• Although the war was over, Evesham left behind ‘disinherited’ rebels whose lands had been confiscated; the Statute of Marlborough (1267) and Edward’s later legal reforms can both be traced back to the unresolved damage of 1265.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance assessed both at the time and over time, with sustained explanation and precise detail.
Secure: Clear discussion of significance with relevant detail and at least two reasons for impact.
Developing: Some significance offered but limited to events at the time, with partial detail.
Emerging: Simple description of the battle with no real discussion of significance.

practice_questions.text: ‘The biggest problem facing Edward I when he became king was the weakness of royal authority left behind by Henry III.’ Evaluate the claim that this is correct
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include arguments in support:
• Henry III’s reign had produced civil war, the Provisions of Oxford and Simon de Montfort’s parliament — all of which set precedents for the magnates to limit royal power.
• Local government had decayed: sheriffs and bailiffs were corrupt, private liberties had expanded, and royal courts had lost business.
• Henry’s reliance on foreign favourites and the Sicilian Business had drained the treasury, leaving Edward financially weak.

Arguments for other problems:
• In Wales, Llywelyn ap Gruffudd refused to attend the coronation or pay homage; this challenge to English overlordship became the immediate crisis of the reign.
• Royal finances were dangerously thin, forcing Edward to rely on Italian bankers and parliamentary taxation from his earliest years.
• The unresolved status of magnate liberties and franchises, dating back to before Henry III, was as serious as Henry’s personal failures — many privileges had been claimed since the Norman Conquest.

Judgement should weigh weakness of royal authority against the Welsh challenge and financial strain, reaching a substantiated conclusion that recognises the inheritance was a connected system of problems rather than separate boxes.

[16 marks]
Mastering: Sustained argument with precise detail, weighed factors and a justified overall judgement that recognises connections between problems.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant detail on more than one factor and a supported judgement.
Developing: Description of more than one factor with limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Single factor described with little or no judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Edward I’s long absence on crusade between 1270 and 1274.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The realm was governed in his name by a council of trusted men — the first time an English king had been recognised as ruler before coronation, which strengthened the constitutional principle that kingship was continuous.
• The crusade gave Edward a Europe-wide reputation as a warrior, especially after surviving an assassination attempt at Acre in 1272; this reputation deterred rebellion when he finally returned.
• His absence delayed urgent reforms: corrupt local officers, decayed royal finances and unresolved baronial liberties were all left to fester until 1274, which is why Edward acted so quickly with the Hundred Rolls inquiry that year.
• The journey home through France and Gascony allowed Edward to pay homage to the king of France for his French lands — a smooth handover that contrasted with Henry III’s troubled relations with the French crown.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained causal explanation linking the crusade absence to multiple later developments, using precise terminology.
Secure: Two effects clearly explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but largely descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements about the crusade with no clear effect on the reign.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Edward I’s character as a king.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Tall, physically imposing and famously a skilled warrior — nicknamed ‘Longshanks’ because of his unusual height and long arms; chroniclers stressed his energy and military leadership.
• Disciplined and hard-working in matters of government, with a strong personal interest in law and statute-making, supported by able ministers such as Robert Burnell.
• Devoutly religious: he had taken the cross and gone on crusade, and saw kingship as a sacred duty to deliver justice.
• Quick-tempered and merciless to anyone he believed had betrayed him; this would later be seen in his treatment of Dafydd ap Gruffudd and the brutal sack of Berwick in 1296.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail. Two clearly separate features required.]

lessons.title: Restoring Royal Authority: The Hundred Rolls and Quo Warranto
lessons.description: Edward’s first inquiry into the state of the kingdom and his challenge to noble privilege.
lessons.content_html:
A Kingdom Under Inspection

Within months of his coronation in 1274, Edward I launched the largest investigation of local government any English king had ever attempted. Royal commissioners were sent into every hundred of every county to ask the same set of questions: what royal lands were missing, which sheriffs had taken bribes, which lords had set up private courts, and which liberties had been claimed without the king’s permission. The replies were written down on long parchment rolls — the Hundred Rolls — and they gave Edward something no previous king had ever possessed: a detailed map of where royal authority had leaked away.

Key Fact

The Hundred Rolls inquiry of 1274–75 sent royal commissioners into every county to gather sworn jury evidence about lost royal rights, corrupt officials and unauthorised baronial liberties. The surviving rolls fill several volumes and remain one of the richest sources for medieval English local life.

Robert Burnell, the Chancellor

The man behind the inquiry was Robert Burnell, Edward’s closest adviser. Burnell had served Edward as a household clerk before the king’s accession and was appointed Lord Chancellor in September 1274. As Lord Chancellor he kept the great seal of England, drafted royal writs, and ran the chancery — the king’s writing office. Contemporary chroniclers described him as wise, cautious and a brilliant lawyer, although critics noted he held many church offices at once and lived in the manner of a great lord. He became Bishop of Bath and Wells in 1275 but continued to dominate royal government until his death in 1292.

Burnell’s genius was administrative. He organised the commissioners, framed the questions they asked, and turned the answers into the legislative programme of the next decade. Almost every great Edwardian statute carries his fingerprints.

Local juries reported corrupt sheriffs taking bribes to ignore crimes, bailiffs charging illegal fees, and great lords running their own courts as if they were kings. They also recorded lost royal lands — pieces of crown estate that had been quietly absorbed by neighbouring lords. In some places jurors were too frightened of their lord to give honest answers, but the picture was clear: royal authority had been thinning out for two generations.

The findings shaped the First Statute of Westminster (1275), the Statute of Gloucester (1278) and the Quo Warranto inquiries that followed. The Hundred Rolls were not just a complaint book — they became the working data behind reform.

‘By What Warrant?’

Once the rolls revealed how many lords claimed private courts and other rights, Edward struck. From 1278, royal justices on circuit began to summon barons and ask them Quo Warranto: by what authority do you hold this market, this gallows, this hundred court? The principle was that all jurisdiction belonged to the crown unless a lord could show a royal grant. Many barons had no charter to wave at the justices — the rights had simply been exercised for so long that everyone had stopped asking.

The Rusty Sword

The most famous Quo Warranto moment came when Earl Warenne was challenged about his liberties. According to the chronicler, the earl drew an old, rust-stained sword and declared, ‘Look, my lords, here is my warrant. My ancestors came with William the Bastard and conquered their lands by the sword, and I will defend them by the sword against anyone who tries to take them.’ Whether or not the speech was made exactly as reported, it captured the mood of the older nobility: they would not let Edward dismantle their franchise rights through paper inquiries.

Edward eventually compromised. The Statute of Quo Warranto (1290) accepted that any liberty exercised continuously since the coronation of Richard I in 1189 was lawful, even without a written charter. Continuous use had become its own warrant. This was a partial royal retreat — barons kept most of what they held — but the king had still asserted, on paper, that all jurisdiction flowed from the crown. The principle would matter when later kings tested the same boundary.

A New Style of Government

The Hundred Rolls and Quo Warranto inquiries together showed how Edward planned to rule: not through dramatic confrontation but through paperwork, evidence and the systematic recovery of lost royal rights. Edward did not destroy the great liberties of the magnates — he could not afford a new civil war — but he established that the crown was now actively monitoring local government in a way that had never been seen before.

Key Fact

The Quo Warranto inquiries from 1278 demanded that barons prove their right to hold private liberties. The Statute of Quo Warranto in 1290 accepted continuous use since 1189 (the coronation of Richard I) as proof — a partial royal retreat that still asserted the principle that all jurisdiction came from the crown.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a ‘Describe Two Features’ question, give two clearly separate features — not one elaborate idea split in half. For example, ‘the Hundred Rolls used royal commissioners visiting every county’ is one feature; ‘they relied on sworn evidence from local juries’ is a second feature. Each feature needs its own supporting detail. Avoid vague phrases like ‘the king made a survey’; use precise terms such as commissioners, hundred, jury and writ.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Hundred Rolls inquiry of 1274–75 was the largest investigation of local government any English king had ever attempted, gathering sworn jury evidence in every county.
  • Robert Burnell, Lord Chancellor 1274–1292, designed the inquiry and turned its findings into the great Edwardian statutes.
  • The Quo Warranto inquiries from 1278 challenged baronial liberties; the Statute of Quo Warranto (1290) accepted continuous use since 1189 as a valid warrant, a compromise that left the principle of royal supremacy intact.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Hundred Rolls inquiry of 1274–75.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Royal commissioners were sent into every hundred of every county and questioned local juries on oath about royal rights, corrupt officials and private liberties.
• The inquiry recorded its findings on long parchment rolls, which gave Edward I a written record of where royal authority had been lost or abused.
• The questions were standardised across the country, drafted in the chancery under Robert Burnell, so that answers could be compared between counties.
• The data fed directly into later legislation, including the First Statute of Westminster (1275) and the Quo Warranto inquiries that began in 1278.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail. Two clearly separate features required.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Quo Warranto inquiries on relations between Edward I and the nobility.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Many barons resented being challenged to prove their right to liberties their families had held for generations — this caused tension between Edward and the older nobility, captured in stories like Earl Warenne’s ‘rusty sword’.
• The inquiries forced barons to look for old charters and royal grants in their muniments rooms; this made the relationship between king and noble more legalistic and document-based, and reduced reliance on custom alone.
• The Statute of Quo Warranto (1290) was a compromise: continuous use since 1189 was accepted as warrant, which calmed baronial anger but still asserted that all jurisdiction came from the crown.
• Edward avoided open rebellion by working with leading magnates such as the earls of Gloucester and Norfolk, but he stored up resentment that would surface later in the reign over taxation and the Welsh and Scottish wars.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of effects on king-noble relations, with explicit causal links and precise vocabulary.
Secure: Two effects clearly explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but explanation is descriptive rather than causal.
Emerging: Simple statements about Quo Warranto with little reference to relations with nobles.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Robert Burnell for Edward I’s government.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Burnell was Lord Chancellor from 1274 until his death in 1292, providing eighteen years of administrative continuity at the heart of royal government.
• He designed the Hundred Rolls inquiry and shaped the great Edwardian statutes, including Westminster I (1275), Gloucester (1278), Mortmain (1279) and Westminster II (1285); without his organising mind, the legislative programme would have been impossible.
• His mastery of the chancery and the great seal turned royal government into a paper machine that could reach every county; the writs that summoned juries, opened pleas and demanded warrants all flowed through his office.
• Over time, the Burnell era set a template for English government: a learned chancellor, a permanent chancery, and a king who governed by statute and writ rather than by personal command alone.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of significance both at the time and over time, with precise terminology.
Secure: Clear discussion of why Burnell mattered, with relevant detail and at least two reasons.
Developing: Some significance discussed but largely descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements about Burnell’s role with no real discussion of significance.

practice_questions.text: ‘The Hundred Rolls inquiry was the most important reform of Edward I’s early reign.’ Evaluate the claim that this is correct
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The inquiry produced the data that drove every other reform: the Statutes of Westminster, Gloucester and Mortmain all responded to evidence gathered in 1274–75.
• It established a new style of government — rule by paper, evidence and standardised questions — which would become a permanent feature of English administration.
• It restored confidence in royal justice by exposing corrupt sheriffs and bailiffs, giving ordinary people reason to trust royal courts again.

Arguments for other reforms:
• The Statute of Westminster I (1275) translated complaints into actual law, banning corruption in juries and protecting widows and tenants.
• The Quo Warranto inquiries challenged baronial liberties directly, which the Hundred Rolls only described.
• The First Statute of Westminster fixed the rules for elections to parliament and is sometimes seen as the foundation of later parliamentary practice.

Judgement should weigh the data-gathering of the Hundred Rolls against the legal change produced by the early statutes, recognising that the inquiry made the reforms possible but that the reforms themselves changed lives.

[16 marks]
Mastering: Sustained argument with weighed factors and a justified overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant detail on more than one factor and a supported judgement.
Developing: Description of more than one factor with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described with no real judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Quo Warranto inquiries.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• From 1278, royal justices on circuit demanded that barons prove the warrant for their private liberties — courts, markets, fairs and hundred jurisdictions.
• The inquiries assumed that all jurisdiction belonged to the crown unless a lord could produce a royal charter or grant.
• The famous response of Earl Warenne — brandishing an old sword as his ‘warrant’ — captured baronial resistance to written-charter standards of proof.
• The Statute of Quo Warranto (1290) accepted continuous use since the coronation of Richard I (1189) as valid warrant.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail. Two clearly separate features required.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Statute of Quo Warranto (1290) for the relationship between the crown and the nobility.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The statute was a compromise: it accepted continuous use since 1189 as proof of warrant, which calmed baronial anger that the king was trying to strip away ancient privileges.
• It still asserted the principle that all jurisdiction flowed from the crown, even where the crown could not actually take it back, which mattered in later disputes between kings and over-mighty subjects.
• The compromise allowed Edward to keep working with leading magnates through the 1290s while he turned to the Welsh and Scottish wars; this is why historians speak of Edward as a constitutional pragmatist rather than a tyrant.
• Over time, the principle of warrant from royal grant shaped how franchises were granted and policed under later medieval kings.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance discussed at the time and over time with sustained causal explanation.
Secure: Clear discussion of significance with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance described but largely tied to immediate effects.
Emerging: Simple statement of what the statute did with no real significance.

lessons.title: Edward the Lawgiver: The Statutes of Westminster, Gloucester and Mortmain
lessons.description: The great Edwardian statutes that reshaped land law, justice and the church.
lessons.content_html:
The Lawgiver King

Edward I has often been called ‘the English Justinian’ because his reign produced the largest body of legislation any English king had attempted. Once the Hundred Rolls had revealed how local government was failing, Edward and his Lord Chancellor Robert Burnell turned the findings into law. Between 1275 and 1290 a series of major statutes reshaped land tenure, criminal justice and the church’s relationship with the crown. These statutes were the spine of Edward’s government and many remained in force for centuries.

Key Fact

The four great Edwardian statutes were Westminster I (1275), Gloucester (1278), Mortmain (1279) and Westminster II (1285). Together they reformed corrupt officials, defined royal jurisdiction, restricted gifts of land to the church, and made it harder to break up family estates.

First Statute of Westminster, 1275

Issued at Edward’s first parliament in April 1275, the First Statute of Westminster bundled together fifty-one chapters of reform. It dealt with abuses uncovered by the Hundred Rolls: corrupt sheriffs, bullying of jurors, the over-use of distraint (seizing a tenant’s livestock or chattels for debt), and the exploitation of widows and minors. It also set rules for free elections to parliament, regulated the costs of legal proceedings and confirmed Magna Carta. The statute was written in French rather than Latin so that more royal officers could read it directly.

Statute of Gloucester, 1278

The Statute of Gloucester opened the Quo Warranto inquiries and gave fresh legal remedies to tenants. It allowed people who had been wrongly thrown out of their land to claim damages as well as the land itself, and it strengthened actions against lords who had carved off pieces of common land. It is often paired with the Hundred Rolls because together they were Edward’s tools for clawing back rights and curbing local oppression.

The medieval church was wealthy. Pious nobles and wealthy townsfolk often gave land to monasteries, cathedrals and friaries to win prayers for their souls. Once land was transferred to the church it was held in mortmain — the ‘dead hand’ — because the church never died, never married and never had heirs. That meant the king lost a long stream of feudal incidents (reliefs, wardships and marriages) that he could normally collect when a tenant died.

By 1279 enough land had drifted into mortmain to become a serious financial worry. The Statute of Mortmain (1279) banned all transfers of land to the church without a royal licence. The licence cost money, so Edward turned a problem into a revenue stream.

Second Statute of Westminster, 1285

The Second Statute of Westminster (1285) was the most far-reaching of all. Its first chapter, De Donis Conditionalibus (‘Concerning Conditional Gifts’), created the legal doctrine of the entail. If a parent gave land ‘to my son and the heirs of his body’, that land could no longer be sold or given away — it had to descend in the family line. This let great families lock down their estates for generations. Other chapters reformed civil procedure, expanded the writ system, and set out new rules for trespass and wrongful occupation.

Westminster II also confirmed something with much wider effects: the Statute of Winchester, also issued in 1285, which reformed local policing. Each man between fifteen and sixty had to keep arms suitable to his rank, and the watch was organised in towns and on highways. Anyone who saw a crime had to raise the hue and cry and join the chase.

Quia Emptores, 1290

The last of the great early statutes was Quia Emptores in 1290. It allowed free tenants to sell their land outright, but the buyer would hold it from the seller’s lord, not from the seller. Over time this stopped the creation of new layers of feudal lordship and simplified the structure of land tenure across England. Together with Mortmain and Westminster II, it tightened the king’s grip on land law.

Historians like Michael Prestwich have argued that the Edwardian statutes turned England into Europe’s most law-bound kingdom. Common law — the law of the king’s courts shared across the whole country — grew under Edward into something recognisable to a modern lawyer. Many provisions of Westminster I, Mortmain and Westminster II were still being cited in English courts in the nineteenth century. Marc Morris adds a darker note: the same king who reformed law for free Englishmen presided over the brutal expulsion of the Jews in 1290, showing that ‘justice’ in this period had hard limits.

Key Fact

The Statute of Mortmain (1279) banned all transfers of land to the church without a royal licence. Edward wanted it because land in church hands escaped the feudal incidents he relied on for income, and the licence fees turned the problem into a profitable royal right.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Significance’ question on the Edwardian statutes, the highest band rewards significance both at the time and over time. At the time: the statutes responded directly to the Hundred Rolls findings and reshaped land and justice. Over time: many provisions remained in force for centuries and shaped the common law tradition. Use exact statute names and years — vague references to ‘Edward’s laws’ will cap your marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Edward I’s great statutes — Westminster I (1275), Gloucester (1278), Mortmain (1279), Westminster II (1285) and Winchester (1285) — reshaped land law, justice and policing.
  • The Statute of Mortmain banned grants of land to the church without royal licence, protecting the king’s feudal income; Westminster II created the entail through De Donis Conditionalibus.
  • Together with Quia Emptores (1290), the statutes earned Edward the nickname ‘the English Justinian’ and shaped English common law for centuries.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Statute of Mortmain (1279) for the relationship between the crown and the church.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the statute stopped wealthy nobles giving large estates to the church without royal permission, protecting the king’s feudal incidents (reliefs, wardships, marriages) which were a major source of revenue.
• It established the principle that the crown had a say in how land moved between lay and religious owners; this asserted royal authority over the church in a sphere where canon law had previously dominated.
• Over time, the licensing system became a steady source of crown income and a model for later regulation of charitable land — the same idea would still be operating under the Tudors.
• The statute fits the wider pattern of Edward’s reform programme: law made in parliament, designed by Robert Burnell, and aimed at recovering rights the crown had lost during Henry III’s reign.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance discussed both at the time and over time with sustained explanation and precise terms.
Secure: Clear discussion of significance with at least two reasons and relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance offered but largely tied to immediate effects.
Emerging: Simple statement of what the statute did with little discussion of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Second Statute of Westminster (1285) on landholding in England.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • Its opening chapter De Donis Conditionalibus created the entail, allowing land to be tied to a particular line of heirs and protected from sale; this caused great families to lock down estates that could not be broken up by an heir. • It expanded the writ system, providing new remedies for trespass and wrongful occupation; this caused more disputes to be channelled into the king’s courts and away from local lords. • Together with the Statute of Winchester (1285) it strengthened policing through the watch and the hue and cry, which caused a more visible royal presence in towns and on highways. • Over time, the entail shaped the structure of English aristocratic estates for centuries, and the wider statute remained a foundation document for the common law. [8 marks] Mastering: Sustained causal explanation with multiple linked effects and precise vocabulary. Secure: Two effects clearly explained with relevant detail. Developing: Effects identified but explanation is largely descriptive. Emerging: Simple statements about the statute with little explanation of effects.

practice_questions.text: ‘Edward I deserves the title “English Justinian” because of his great statutes.’ Evaluate the claim that this is correct
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: • The statutes between 1275 and 1290 are the largest body of royal legislation any English king had produced; many provisions of Westminster I and Westminster II were still cited in English courts in the nineteenth century. • The statutes turned the findings of the Hundred Rolls into permanent law, addressing corruption, land disputes, mortmain and policing in a single legislative programme. • The doctrine of the entail (De Donis Conditionalibus) and Quia Emptores reshaped land tenure for centuries, fitting the ‘lawgiver’ comparison. Arguments against / for other achievements: • Edward also reformed parliament — the ‘Model Parliament’ of 1295 broadened representation, even if not for democratic reasons. • His military achievements in Wales (Statute of Rhuddlan 1284) were as transformative for British politics as any law of land tenure. • Critics like Marc Morris note that ‘justice’ under Edward had hard limits — the 1290 expulsion of the Jews and the brutal punishment of Dafydd ap Gruffudd suggest a darker side that the ‘English Justinian’ nickname can obscure. Judgement should weigh the legislative achievement against military and constitutional change, recognising that the statutes were genuinely transformative but were one part of a broader reign. [16 marks] Mastering: Sustained argument with weighed factors and a justified overall judgement. Secure: Clear argument with relevant detail on multiple factors and a supported judgement. Developing: Description of more than one factor with limited weighing. Emerging: Single factor described with no real judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Statute of Winchester (1285) for law and order in medieval England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the statute organised the watch in towns and on highways, requiring every adult man to keep arms suitable to his rank; this gave local communities a structured role in catching criminals.
• It re-stated the duty of the hue and cry: anyone who witnessed a crime was bound to shout an alarm and join the chase, with collective responsibility on the whole hundred for unsolved offences.
• Over time, the statute’s framework for community policing remained the basis of English local law enforcement until the creation of professional police forces in the nineteenth century.
• It is significant alongside the Hundred Rolls and Westminster II as one part of a coordinated programme of legal reform: gathering data, then writing law, then enforcing law in the localities.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance discussed both at the time and over time, with sustained explanation.
Secure: Clear discussion of significance with relevant detail and at least two reasons.
Developing: Some significance described but largely tied to immediate effects.
Emerging: Simple statement of what the statute did with no discussion of significance.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Statute of Mortmain (1279).
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:

• It protected the king’s feudal incidents — the reliefs, wardships and marriages collected when lay tenants died — which the church never owed.
• Royal licences could be granted for a fee, turning the rule into a source of crown revenue.
• It applied to all churches, abbeys and friaries, including the new Franciscan and Dominican houses.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail. Two clearly separate features required.]

lessons.title: Wool, Banks and the Royal Purse
lessons.description: How agriculture, the wool trade and Italian bankers funded Edward I’s ambitions.
lessons.content_html:
A Kingdom Built on Wool

Thirteenth-century England was a farming country, and its richest export by far was wool. The damp grasslands of the Cotswolds, Lincolnshire, the Welsh borders and the Yorkshire moors fed flocks that fleeced some of the finest wool in Europe. Most was shipped through London, Boston and Hull to Flemish weavers in Bruges and Ghent, who turned it into cloth and sold it back across Europe. Edward I understood that whoever controlled this trade controlled the kingdom’s wealth. His financial system was built on it.

Key Fact

Edward I’s royal finance rested on three pillars: the wool customs (‘maltolt’) introduced in 1275, loans from Italian banking houses (the Riccardi of Lucca, then the Frescobaldi of Florence), and parliamentary grants of taxation. Together they paid for the Welsh wars, castle programme and Scottish campaigns.

The Wool Customs of 1275

At his first parliament in April 1275, Edward asked the merchants and barons to grant him a customs duty on wool exports. They agreed: half a mark (six shillings and eightpence) on every sack leaving an English port, with a smaller duty on hides. This was the ‘Ancient Custom’ — a steady, predictable income paid by exporters at the dockside. The duty was light enough that wool merchants tolerated it, and it brought in roughly £10,000 a year — a transformative addition to royal revenue.

In 1294, with war breaking out against France and rebellion in Wales, Edward demanded a far heavier maltolt — literally ‘the bad tax’ in Anglo-French — of forty shillings on every sack, six times the ordinary rate. Merchants protested, calling the levy crippling and ruinous, and the maltolt became a flashpoint in the political crisis of 1297 that forced Edward to confirm Magna Carta and accept new limits on his powers.

The Riccardi of Lucca

Customs revenue was steady but not enough on its own to fund a war. For credit, Edward turned to Italy. From 1272 the Riccardi of Lucca became royal bankers. They lent on a far larger scale than English moneylenders could, and they were paid back through the wool customs — the king redirected the duty straight to them at the ports until the loans were cleared. Between 1272 and 1294 the Riccardi advanced around £400,000 to the crown, financing the first Welsh war, the early Welsh castle programme and Edward’s diplomatic missions.

The system collapsed in 1294. War with France meant French royal officers seized Riccardi assets in Paris; at the same moment Edward froze their English accounts to fund his own campaigns. The bank could not survive losing both ends and went bankrupt. Edward turned almost immediately to a new house from Florence, the Frescobaldi, who took over royal lending until they too crashed in 1311 under Edward II.

Medieval Christian teaching forbade Christians to lend at interest, calling the practice usury. Italian banking houses found ways around this through bills of exchange, partnership contracts and currency-conversion fees that produced profit without naming it as interest. They also operated on a continental scale — the Riccardi could collect debts in France, Flanders and the papal court — which English moneylenders could not match. Once Edward’s Jewish lenders had been pushed out of moneylending by the 1275 Statute of the Jewry, the Italians were the only credit network big enough to finance a king at war.

The Great Re-Coinage, 1279–80

The English silver penny had been the only coin in regular use since the eleventh century, and after generations of clipping, sweating and counterfeiting most pennies in circulation were short of their proper weight. In 1279 Edward ordered a complete re-coinage. Old coins were called in and melted down. New pennies were struck on a heavier flan with a larger inscription that made clipping obvious; he also introduced a four-penny groat and a quarter-penny farthing for the first time. The scheme paid for itself through the seigniorage — the small profit the mint took from each coin — and gave merchants a trustworthy currency that supported the wool trade.

The Statute of Merchants, 1285

Edward’s government also wrote rules to make trade safer for creditors. The Statute of Merchants of 1285 (an extension of an earlier 1283 Statute of Acton Burnell) let creditors register a debt before the mayor of a chartered town. If the debt was not paid by the agreed date, the creditor could seize the debtor’s movable goods and, after three months, his lands as well. For a wool merchant in Boston or a draper in Lincoln, the new procedure was revolutionary: it turned credit, the engine of commerce, into a faster, more enforceable contract. Foreign merchants gained too, encouraging Italian and Flemish buyers to pay English producers up front for next year’s wool clip.

Most wool changed hands at the great fairs — St Ives, Stamford, Boston, Winchester and Northampton — where Italian and Flemish buyers met English producers. Towns chartered by the Crown to hold weekly markets and annual fairs paid the king for the privilege; in return their citizens enjoyed legal protections under the borough customs. Edward extended this network throughout his reign, granting hundreds of new market charters. Each one widened the kingdom’s tax base.

Key Fact

The 1275 wool customs of half a mark per sack brought in around £10,000 a year and were used to repay loans from the Riccardi of Lucca. The much heavier maltolt of 1294 — six times the ordinary rate — helped pay for the Madog rising in Wales and the start of the Scottish campaigns, but provoked a serious political crisis in 1297.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Effects’ question on wool, banks and royal finance, examiners want a chain of cause and effect — not three separate paragraphs. Show how the 1275 wool customs gave Edward steady income, how that income secured loans from the Riccardi, how those loans paid for the Welsh wars, and how the collapse of the Riccardi in 1294 forced the heavier maltolt that caused the political crisis of 1297. Use precise sums (£10,000, £400,000) and named bankers to anchor your answer.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • English wool was the kingdom’s main export; the 1275 wool customs of half a mark per sack gave Edward roughly £10,000 a year and the heavier 1294 maltolt provoked a major political crisis.
  • The Riccardi of Lucca lent around £400,000 to the crown between 1272 and 1294, secured against the wool customs; the Frescobaldi of Florence took over after the Riccardi collapsed.
  • The 1279–80 re-coinage produced a trustworthy currency, while the Statute of Merchants (1285) gave creditors a fast procedure to seize debtors’ goods and lands.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the wool customs introduced by Edward I in 1275.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The duty was set at half a mark (six shillings and eightpence) per sack of wool exported, with a smaller duty on hides.
• It was paid by exporters at the dockside in London, Boston, Hull and other ports as the wool left for Flanders.
• It brought in around £10,000 a year, a transformative new source of royal income.
• It was granted by parliament with the consent of merchants, making it the ‘Ancient Custom’ on which later wool taxation was built.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the collapse of the Riccardi of Lucca in 1294 on Edward I’s government.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Crown lost its main source of credit just as war with France and the Madog rising in Wales required heavy military spending.
• Edward demanded the maltolt of 1294 — forty shillings a sack, six times the ordinary rate — on wool exporters, which produced an outcry from English merchants.
• The Florentine Frescobaldi were drafted in to replace the Riccardi, transferring royal credit from one Italian house to another but on tighter terms.
• The combined pressure of the maltolt, French war and Welsh rising fed into the political crisis of 1297, when Edward had to confirm Magna Carta and accept limits on tax-raising.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Multiple causal links developed with precise figures and named bankers.
Secure: Two or more effects clearly explained with supporting detail.
Developing: Effects identified but explanation is largely descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements about the collapse with little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Great Re-Coinage of 1279–80 for trade in Edward I’s England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:

• The introduction of the groat (4d) and farthing (quarter-penny) gave merchants more flexible denominations for everyday trade.
• The seigniorage profit collected by the mint paid for the operation, so it strengthened the Crown without an unpopular new tax.
• Significance over time: a trustworthy currency was essential for the wool trade and for the credit deals with Italian bankers; the new coin standards lasted into the fourteenth century.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.

Students may include:

• After three months of non-payment, the creditor could also seize the debtor’s lands.
• It extended an earlier 1283 Statute of Acton Burnell, building a national network of registered debts.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the wool trade on Edward I’s ability to wage war.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Customs duties on wool gave Edward a steady cash income that he could pledge to Italian bankers for far larger loans.
• The Riccardi of Lucca advanced around £400,000 between 1272 and 1294, repaid through wool customs at the ports — this paid for the first Welsh war and the early castle programme.
• When wartime needs spiked in 1294, the maltolt squeezed the trade six times harder, funding the Madog rising response and the early Scottish campaigns.
• Heavy reliance on wool also created political risk: the merchant outcry of 1297 forced Edward to confirm Magna Carta and limit future taxation without consent.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Multiple effects developed with precise figures and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Two or more effects explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using examples from across Edward I’s reign, that the wool trade was the most important factor in shaping his government.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The 1275 wool customs of half a mark per sack created the steady income that secured loans from the Riccardi of Lucca, financing the Welsh wars.
• The Riccardi collapse in 1294 and the maltolt that replaced it triggered the constitutional crisis of 1297, forcing the confirmation of Magna Carta.
• The 1279–80 re-coinage and the Statute of Merchants (1285) were both designed to keep the trade flowing safely through English ports.
• Wool revenue paid for both the Iron Ring castle programme in Wales and the Scottish campaigns, making it the financial backbone of the reign.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Parliamentary grants of taxation also funded military campaigns, including the £116,000 grant linked to the 1290 expulsion of the Jews.
• The Hundred Rolls, Quo Warranto and the great statutes (Westminster I, II, Mortmain, Winchester) shaped government in ways unrelated to wool.
• Edward’s personal authority and his use of Robert Burnell as Lord Chancellor mattered as much as any single revenue source.
• The conquest of Wales had political and dynastic motives beyond money — Llywelyn’s defiance and the desire to settle the British Isles.

A strong response weighs the wool-trade factor against the legal, parliamentary and personal aspects of Edward’s government and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

[16 marks]
Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on multiple factors and a supported judgement.
Developing: Description of more than one factor with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described with no real judgement.

lessons.title: Crime, Courts and Punishment in Edward's England
lessons.description: How royal justice reached every village through courts, juries and brutal medieval punishments.
lessons.content_html:
The Reach of the King’s Justice

When Edward I came to the throne in 1272, the king’s justice was already the most centralised in Europe. Henry II had built a system of royal courts, royal writs and travelling judges that could pull cases out of local lords’ hands and into the king’s. Edward inherited this machine and sharpened it. By the 1280s a peasant in a Lincolnshire village or a merchant in a Cornish port could expect a royal judge to ride into his county at least once every few years to hear major crimes. The result was a kingdom where the law of the land — what historians later called the common law — really did reach into the localities.

Key Fact

Three main royal courts sat at Westminster under Edward I: King’s Bench (criminal cases involving the Crown and serious felonies), Common Pleas (civil disputes between subjects, especially over land), and the Exchequer of Pleas (cases concerning royal revenue and the king’s debtors).

The Royal Courts at Westminster

By Edward’s reign three permanent benches met at Westminster. The Court of King’s Bench handled major criminal cases and offences against the king. The Court of Common Pleas dealt with civil disputes between subjects, especially over land. The Exchequer of Pleas handled cases concerning royal revenue. Each had its own chief justice, its own clerks and its own books of pleadings, with judgements gradually building up the case law that lawyers cited for centuries.

Most ordinary people, though, never travelled to Westminster. The king’s justice came to them. Travelling judges — the eyre — toured the counties in great circuits, hearing every Crown plea outstanding. The eyre was a major event: it pulled together every coroner’s roll, every escaped prisoner, every claim of liberty. Because it was so heavy, by Edward’s reign the eyre was being supplemented by faster assize commissions, which dealt with specific cases on a short list and could be issued more often.

From Trial by Ordeal to Trial by Jury

In 1215 the Pope had banned clergy from taking part in trial by ordeal, which had relied on a priest blessing the iron or the water. English judges responded by turning to the jury — twelve men of the neighbourhood who decided whether an accused was guilty. By Edward’s reign trial by jury was the standard route for serious crime. There were two stages: a presenting jury (called the grand jury) listed those suspected of crimes, and a trial jury (the petit jury) decided whether each was guilty. Witnesses were sometimes called, but the jurors were expected to know local reputations themselves — a far more local kind of justice than today’s.

A defendant who refused to plead at all could be sentenced to peine forte et dure — pressed under heavy stones until they pleaded or died. The system was harsh, but it was at least public, regular and (compared with the older ordeals) rational.

The most serious crimes were felonies — murder, robbery, rape, arson, treason — punished by death and forfeiture of all the convict’s goods to the Crown. Less serious offences were trespasses, dealt with by fines, the pillory or the stocks. Treason was a special category that grew under Edward: the punishment of hanging, drawing and quartering used on Dafydd ap Gruffudd in 1283 was extended to a wider range of treasonable crimes by his grandson’s Statute of Treasons in 1352, but its origin lies firmly in this reign. Most petty wrongs were tried in the manor court of the local lord, where the lord’s steward and a jury of villagers fined offenders or set them in the stocks.

The Statute of Winchester, 1285

In October 1285 Edward issued the Statute of Winchester, the most significant piece of legislation on local policing in the medieval period. It built on the older Anglo-Saxon system of frankpledge — collective responsibility — and gave it teeth.

Every man between fifteen and sixty had to keep arms suited to his rank, from a knight’s sword and lance down to a peasant’s bow and arrows. A formal watch was set in each town, with gates closed at sunset; strangers entering after dark could be arrested. When a crime was reported, anyone hearing the alarm had to raise the hue and cry and join the chase. If the criminal was not caught, the whole hundred — the local administrative district — was collectively fined. Crucially, hedges and undergrowth within 200 feet of major roads had to be cleared so that highwaymen had nowhere to hide.

Punishment as Public Spectacle

Medieval punishment was meant to be seen. Petty offenders — thieves, fraudsters and brewers selling short measures — were placed in the pillory in the market place, where neighbours could mock or pelt them with rotten food. The stocks held offenders by the feet. Felons sentenced to death were hanged at the town gallows, often on market day, so that the largest possible crowd would witness the sentence. Bodies were sometimes left to rot in chains as a warning to travellers.

For the most extreme cases of treason, Edward devised a new punishment. In 1283 Dafydd ap Gruffudd, brother of Llywelyn, was the first English nobleman to be hanged, drawn and quartered: dragged on a hurdle to the gallows, hanged but cut down alive, disembowelled, beheaded and his body cut into four parts to be displayed on city gates. The brutality was deliberate. Edward wanted treason against the Crown to look qualitatively different from any other crime, and the punishment was extended in later reigns to a wider list of treasonable offences.

Key Fact

The Statute of Winchester (1285) required every man aged 15 to 60 to keep arms suitable to his rank, organised the watch in towns and on highways, and made the local hundred collectively liable for unsolved offences. It remained the framework of English policing until the creation of professional police forces in the nineteenth century.

For example, ‘the eyre toured the counties’ and ‘the King’s Bench sat at Westminster’ are two clean features, each of which can take a supporting detail. One elaborate paragraph on the eyre alone will lose half the marks. Use precise medieval terms (eyre, assize, frankpledge, hue and cry, pillory) wherever you can.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Three royal courts — King’s Bench, Common Pleas and Exchequer of Pleas — sat at Westminster, while the eyre and the assize judges took the king’s justice into the counties.
  • Trial by jury had replaced trial by ordeal after 1215; juries presented suspects (grand jury) and decided guilt (petit jury) using local knowledge.
  • The Statute of Winchester (1285) organised local policing through frankpledge, the watch and the hue and cry; punishment was a public spectacle, with felons hanged and traitors hanged, drawn and quartered.

lessons.title: Faith and Learning: The Church, Universities and Roger Bacon
lessons.description: The thirteenth-century church, Oxford and Cambridge, and the rise of medieval English learning.
lessons.content_html:
A Church at the Heart of Daily Life

Every parish in Edward I’s England gathered in a stone church on Sunday. The medieval Church taught children, kept the calendar, recorded births and deaths, fed the poor, and offered the sacraments through which souls reached heaven. The Pope in Rome appointed England’s archbishops and bishops, and English kings sometimes clashed with him over taxation and appointments. By Edward’s reign two old religious orders — the Benedictines and Cistercians — were being challenged from within by a new and more austere kind of clergy: the friars.

Key Fact

Two main orders of friars arrived in England in the 1220s: the Franciscans (founded by St Francis of Assisi, called Greyfriars from their grey habit) preached poverty and humility; the Dominicans (founded by St Dominic, called Blackfriars from their black cloak) emphasised study and preaching against heresy.

The Friars in Edward’s England

Unlike monks, who lived enclosed in monasteries, friars lived among lay people. They went barefoot through town streets, begged for their bread and preached in the open air. They settled deliberately in the rough, growing parts of England’s cities — Greyfriars in Newgate in London, Blackfriars next to the Thames at Ludgate, similar houses at Oxford, Cambridge, York and Norwich. The Franciscans were valued for their simplicity; the Dominicans, often university trained, became the leading preachers and confessors of their day.

Edward used the friars too. They preached the cause of the crusades, served as ambassadors and were among the voices urging him toward the 1290 expulsion of the Jews. By the end of his reign, every major town in England had at least one friary and the friars had become a familiar part of the urban landscape.

The Rise of the Universities

Oxford and Cambridge had grown out of cathedral schools in the twelfth century. By Edward’s reign both were established universities. Students arrived as young as thirteen and worked through the seven liberal arts (grammar, rhetoric, logic, arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy) before moving on to higher faculties of theology, canon law, civil law or medicine. Most teaching was in Latin and almost all students were in minor orders — clerks of the Church — even if they never became full priests.

Lectures were free; what students paid for was lodging and food in the masters’ halls. To bring order, wealthy patrons began endowing halls of residence with their own statutes — the first medieval colleges. Colleges at Oxford grew quickly: Merton (1264, refounded by Walter de Merton 1274), Balliol (founded by John de Balliol’s widow Dervorguilla in the 1260s, statutes 1282), and University College (which traced itself to a 1249 endowment). At Cambridge, Peterhouse was founded in 1284 by the Bishop of Ely. These colleges fixed Oxford and Cambridge into stable institutions that would dominate English higher learning for centuries.

The undergraduate course took six or seven years. Students attended lectures, where a master read aloud from a set text such as Aristotle’s logic, and disputations, where they argued formal questions on either side of a problem. The dominant intellectual method was scholasticism — setting authoritative texts (the Bible, the Church Fathers, Aristotle) against each other and reconciling them through tight reasoning. A bachelor’s degree required candidates to defend their answers in formal debate; a master’s required them to lecture for two years.

Roger Bacon and Experimental Science

The most famous English scholar of the age was the Franciscan Roger Bacon (c.1219–1292), known as ‘Doctor Mirabilis’ or the ‘wonderful doctor’. Bacon studied at Oxford and Paris, joined the Franciscans in the 1250s, and produced a vast body of writing on mathematics, optics, astronomy and the philosophy of language. In 1267, at the request of Pope Clement IV, he produced his masterwork the Opus Majus — the ‘Greater Work’ — arguing that Christian learning had to combine scripture, languages, mathematics and experimental science.

Bacon’s emphasis on experiment and direct observation was unusual for his age and earned him a controversial reputation. He proposed magnifying lenses, theorised about flying machines and gunpowder, and corrected the calendar long before his ideas were accepted. His Franciscan order distrusted his independence and at one point placed him under restriction, but his writings became a foundation reference for the experimental tradition centuries later.

Duns Scotus and the ‘Subtle Doctor’

A second towering figure of the late thirteenth century was the Scotsman John Duns Scotus (c.1266–1308), who studied and lectured at Oxford in the 1290s before moving to Paris. He earned the title ‘Doctor Subtilis’ — the Subtle Doctor — for the precision of his reasoning. Where Bacon emphasised experiment, Scotus refined philosophical theology, exploring how individual things could be known and arguing for the immaculate conception of the Virgin Mary — a doctrine the Church only formally accepted six centuries later. Scotus’s work was so dominant in fifteenth- and sixteenth-century universities that those who rejected it were nicknamed ‘Dunsmen’ — the origin of the modern word ‘dunce’.

Edward’s relations with the Papacy were not always smooth. The 1279 Statute of Mortmain limited the Church’s ability to acquire land in England without royal licence, asserting royal authority over a sphere previously dominated by canon law. In 1296, Pope Boniface VIII issued the bull papal bull Clericis Laicos forbidding lay rulers to tax the clergy without papal consent. Edward, deep in war with France and Scotland, simply outlawed any clergyman who refused to pay; many clergy quickly relented. The episode showed how willing Edward was to defy Rome when royal finance demanded it.

Key Fact

Roger Bacon (c.1219–1292) was the Franciscan author of the Opus Majus (1267), pushing for experiment and observation in Christian learning. John Duns Scotus (c.1266–1308), the ‘Subtle Doctor’, refined philosophical theology at Oxford and shaped university teaching for the following two centuries.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Significance’ question on education and learning, examiners want significance both at the time and over time. At the time: the friars and the new colleges remade religious life and higher education within a single generation. Over time: Oxford and Cambridge are the only English universities to keep their medieval college structure, and Bacon’s push for experiment fed into the much later scientific revolution. Use precise names (Merton, Balliol, Peterhouse) and dates (Opus Majus 1267, Peterhouse 1284) wherever you can.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Franciscans (Greyfriars) and Dominicans (Blackfriars) brought a new, public form of religious life to thirteenth-century English towns and worked closely with the universities.
  • Oxford and Cambridge developed into stable universities under Edward I, with the first colleges — Merton, Balliol, University and Peterhouse — founded by 1284.
  • Roger Bacon’s Opus Majus (1267) argued for experimental science within Christian learning, while Duns Scotus, the ‘Subtle Doctor’, dominated philosophical theology in the 1290s.

lessons.title: The Expulsion of the Jews, 1290
lessons.description: The Statute of the Jewry, mounting persecution and Edward’s edict expelling England’s.
lessons.content_html:
A Community in Royal Hands

The Jewish community of medieval England arrived after the Norman Conquest of 1066 and lived under direct royal protection. Successive kings used Jews as a financial resource: only Jews were legally permitted to lend money at interest, a practice the Church called usury. In return for this protection the king could tax Jews directly, without parliamentary consent, through a special levy called tallage. By 1272 the Jewish population was perhaps 2,000 to 3,000 people, concentrated in towns such as London, York, Lincoln, Norwich and Oxford.

Key Fact

England’s Jews lived under direct royal protection. The king could tax them through tallage without consulting Parliament, and they were the only group legally permitted to charge interest on loans — making them indispensable to royal finance until alternatives appeared.

Centuries of Persecution Before 1290

Persecution did not begin with Edward I. In 1144 the murder of a boy in Norwich produced the first blood libel in Europe — the false accusation that Jews killed Christian children for ritual purposes. The cult of ‘Little Saint Hugh of Lincoln’ in 1255 followed the same pattern, and nineteen Jews were hanged. In 1190 a violent pogrom at Clifford’s Tower in York saw 150 Jews killed or driven to suicide. From 1218 English Jews were forced to wear a yellow badge, and after 1255 Henry III sold his rights over the Jewish community to his brother Richard of Cornwall to settle royal debts.

The Statute of the Jewry, 1275

In 1275 Edward I issued the Statute of the Jewry. Its terms transformed Jewish life. Lending money at interest was now banned outright; existing debts were to be reduced. Jews were ordered to take up trade, farming or skilled crafts — occupations from which Christian guilds had long excluded them. They had to wear a larger yellow felt badge in the shape of the Tablets of the Law, and they were taxed at three pence a head from age twelve. Synagogues were restricted to a small list of named towns.

The Statute placed an impossible burden on the community. Cut off from their traditional livelihood and locked out of Christian craft guilds, many Jews fell into poverty. Some turned to coin clipping — shaving silver from the edges of pennies — for which 269 Jews were hanged in London in 1278. The community that remained was poor, vulnerable and visibly marked.

From the 1270s Edward turned to Italian banking houses, especially the Riccardi of Lucca, to finance his wars and building programmes. The Riccardi could lend on a far larger scale than English Jews and were not seen as religiously suspect. Once the king had a richer source of credit, the Jewish community lost the practical value that had previously protected it.

The Edict of Expulsion, 18 July 1290

On 18 July 1290 Edward issued the Edict of Expulsion. Every Jew in England was ordered to leave the country by 1 November, the feast of All Saints. Those who remained could be killed without penalty. Royal officials were instructed to allow the exiles to take portable goods and small sums of money, but their houses, debts and synagogues passed to the Crown. Around 2,000 to 3,000 people were forced into ships at the Cinque Ports; some captains, paid by the head, robbed and drowned passengers in the Thames estuary.

The expulsion was not a sudden whim. It was announced in Parliament alongside a grant of taxation worth roughly £116,000 — the largest single grant of Edward’s reign. The grateful Commons were trading money for the removal of a community their leaders had long resented. Edward had also been pressed by his mother Eleanor of Provence and by the friars, and had practised the policy first in his lands in Gascony, expelling Jews there in 1287.

Key Fact

The 1290 expulsion was both an act of religious intolerance and a financial deal. Edward gained a parliamentary grant of around £116,000 plus the seized property of expelled Jews, while Parliament secured a popular policy. Roughly 2,000–3,000 Jews left England by 1 November 1290.

Aftermath and Significance

England was the first European kingdom to expel its Jewish community. France followed in 1306 and Spain in 1492. The English ban lasted 366 years — Jews were not formally readmitted until Oliver Cromwell allowed their return in 1656. For Edward’s reign the immediate effect was financial: a one-off windfall, a popular taxation grant and the symbolic image of a Christian king cleansing his realm. The longer effect was a country with no openly practising Jewish community for over three centuries, which shaped English religious culture into the modern period.

Historians disagree on how to weigh the 1290 expulsion. Marc Morris stresses Edward’s personal antisemitism and the brutal treatment of those he expelled. Michael Prestwich emphasises the political bargain with Parliament and the king’s shift to Italian credit. Modern Jewish historians such as Robin Mundill see deeper cultural prejudice running through the previous century, of which the Statute of 1275 and the expulsion of 1290 were the climax. All three views agree that the decision was permanent in its effect on English religious life.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Significance’ question on the expulsion of the Jews, examiners want significance both at the time (financial windfall, popular tax grant, religious symbolism) and over time (366-year ban, the model copied by France in 1306 and Spain in 1492). Avoid simply describing what happened — always link the event back to a clear consequence and use precise figures such as the £116,000 grant.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Statute of the Jewry (1275) banned Jewish moneylending, forced badge-wearing and pushed the community into poverty — setting up the conditions for later expulsion.
  • The Edict of Expulsion of 18 July 1290 was both religious and financial: Edward gained a parliamentary tax grant of around £116,000 plus seized Jewish property, while Italian bankers replaced Jewish lenders.
  • England was the first kingdom to expel its Jews; the ban lasted 366 years until Oliver Cromwell allowed their return in 1656.

lessons.title: Medieval Warfare: Cavalry, Castles and Crossbows
lessons.description: The tactics, weapons and technology of late thirteenth-century warfare in Edward I’s armies.
lessons.content_html:
War as the King’s Business

Edward I spent thirty-five years at war — with Wales, with Scotland and with France. Medieval warfare was expensive, slow and shaped by the technology of the day. England did not have a standing army. Instead the king summoned a levied army for each campaign, made up of knights, men-at-arms, archers, crossbowmen and foot-soldiers, paid by the Crown only for the days they served. Understanding how these forces fought helps explain why the Welsh wars succeeded but the Scottish wars dragged on without a final victory.

Key Fact

Edward’s armies combined four main groups: heavy cavalry of knights and men-at-arms, mass infantry of foot-soldiers, longbow archers (mainly from south Wales and Cheshire) and crossbowmen. No one group could win alone — the test of a commander was making them work together.

Cavalry: Knights and Men-at-Arms

The most prestigious part of any army was the heavy cavalry. A knight rode a powerful warhorse, wore mail or partial plate armour and carried a lance, sword and shield. Below the knights came the men-at-arms — professional soldiers, similarly equipped, who fought for wages rather than feudal duty. A charge of massed cavalry could shatter an enemy line that lacked discipline. At Falkirk in 1298 it was the cavalry pursuit, after the Welsh archers had broken Wallace’s schiltrons, that decided the battle.

Cavalry had limits. Horses were expensive: a quality warhorse could cost the equivalent of several years’ wages for a foot-soldier. Knights needed grooms, squires and a string of remounts. They were also vulnerable to disciplined infantry on bad ground — as the English would discover at Stirling Bridge in 1297, where the Scots caught the cavalry on a narrow crossing and destroyed it before it could form up.

Infantry, Longbows and Crossbows

The bulk of an Edwardian army was infantry: foot-soldiers raised by commissions of array from the shires and Welsh marches. Their main weapons were spears, short swords and axes. More valuable still were the missile troops. The English longbow, made of yew and roughly six feet long, could be drawn to the ear and could send a heavy arrow through mail at 200 yards. A trained archer could shoot ten or more arrows a minute. Most English longbowmen of Edward’s reign came from south Wales and Cheshire — areas with a deep-rooted bowman tradition.

The crossbow was a horizontal, mechanically-drawn weapon. It was more powerful than the longbow at short range and required less training, but it was slower to reload — perhaps two bolts a minute compared with ten longbow arrows. Edward employed Genoese and Gascon crossbowmen for siegework, where they could shelter behind a wooden shield called a pavise while reloading.

At Falkirk in July 1298 William Wallace formed his Scottish spearmen into four schiltrons — tight defensive circles bristling with twelve-foot spears. The English heavy cavalry could not break them. Edward then ordered his Welsh and English longbow archers forward. Volley after volley fell on the static Scottish formations until the schiltrons disintegrated. Only at this point did the cavalry charge home. Falkirk is often cited as the moment when massed longbow archery became central to English battle tactics — a doctrine that would dominate the Hundred Years War a generation later.

Armour: From Mail to Plate

In the late thirteenth century armour was changing. The standard knightly defence was a long mail hauberk — thousands of riveted iron rings — worn over a padded gambeson. By Edward’s reign this was beginning to be reinforced with plate: rectangular iron plates riveted inside a leather coat (the ‘coat of plates’), then separate metal plates strapped over the shins, knees and elbows. A foot-soldier could rarely afford much more than a padded jack and a simple iron helmet. The growing weight of plate would, over the next century, change cavalry tactics across Europe.

Siege Warfare

Most medieval campaigns were sieges, not battles. A castle could deny an enemy a region until it was taken. Edward’s armies used four main siege techniques. Mining meant tunnelling under a wall, propping the tunnel with timber, then burning the props so the wall collapsed. Sapping picked away at the masonry under cover of wooden screens. Scaling used ladders and movable wooden towers to attack the walls directly. Bombardment used stone-throwing engines: the trebuchet, powered by a heavy counterweight, and the smaller mangonel, powered by twisted rope.

Edward took these tools to a new scale. At Stirling Castle in 1304 he had a giant trebuchet called ‘Warwolf’ built on the spot; the garrison surrendered before it was even fired, but Edward insisted on a demonstration anyway. A siege ended only when defenders ran out of food, surrendered to spare their lives, or had a breach forced. The longer the siege, the higher the cost in money, men and time — reasons why Edward built ring after ring of stone castles in Wales rather than fight repeated field campaigns.

Key Fact

Edwardian siege warfare used four main techniques: mining (tunnelling and burning), sapping (cutting away masonry), scaling (ladders and towers) and bombardment (trebuchets and mangonels). Most campaigns were sieges, not battles, and the cost of a long siege explains why Edward’s castle programme aimed to make Welsh resistance impossible.
