Avoid stacking two cavalry points or two siege points.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Edwardian armies combined heavy cavalry, mass infantry, longbow archers and crossbowmen — balance between them, not any single arm, won battles.
  • The Welsh longbow proved decisive at Falkirk in 1298, breaking Wallace’s schiltrons and pointing the way to fourteenth-century English tactics.
  • Most campaigns were sieges, fought with mining, sapping, scaling and bombardment by trebuchets and mangonels — explaining why Edward’s castle programme was central to the Welsh conquest.

lessons.title: Conquering Wales: The Wars of 1277 and 1282-83
lessons.description: From Llywelyn’s defiance to the death of the last native Prince of Wales and the Iron Ring of castles.
lessons.content_html:
A Border Problem Edward Inherited

When Edward I returned from crusade in 1274 to be crowned, the most powerful Welsh ruler was Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, Prince of Wales. By the Treaty of Montgomery (1267) Henry III had recognised Llywelyn as overlord of most of native Wales, in return for an annual tribute and an act of homage to the English king. Llywelyn refused to perform this homage to the new king five times between 1274 and 1276. He also refused to surrender his brother Dafydd, who had fled to England after a failed plot, and announced his intention to marry Eleanor de Montfort, daughter of the rebel Simon de Montfort. To Edward this was open defiance.

Key Fact

Edward’s war of 1277 grew from Llywelyn’s repeated refusal to perform homage, his shelter of his rebel brother Dafydd and his planned marriage to the daughter of Simon de Montfort. From the king’s view, the prince of Wales had broken every condition of the 1267 Treaty of Montgomery.

The First Welsh War, 1277

In November 1276 Edward declared Llywelyn a rebel and began preparing a campaign. The army that crossed the border in summer 1277 was unlike any earlier English force in Wales. Three columns advanced, supported by a fleet from the Cinque Ports that controlled the sea around Anglesey. Edward used hundreds of foresters to clear roads through the Welsh woodlands so that his cavalry and supplies could move. Anglesey, the ‘granary of Snowdonia’, was occupied. Cut off from his harvest, Llywelyn was starved into surrender by November.

The first war ended with the Treaty of Aberconwy. Llywelyn kept the title Prince of Wales but lost most of his lands east of the Conwy River, and was reduced to a small principality of Gwynedd. He performed homage to Edward at Westminster in 1278. The Crown began building a first ring of castles — Flint, Rhuddlan, Builth and Aberystwyth — to garrison the new royal lands.

The Second Welsh War, 1282–83

The peace did not last. On Palm Sunday 1282, Llywelyn’s brother Dafydd, who had switched sides to Edward in 1277 and felt his rewards were inadequate, attacked the English-held Hawarden Castle and massacred its garrison. Other Welsh princes joined him. Llywelyn, surprised by the rising, was forced into a war he had not chosen. Edward’s response was overwhelming — an army of more than 15,000 men, paid for in part by loans from the Riccardi of Lucca and a tax on the wool trade.

The decisive moment came on 11 December 1282 at Cilmeri in mid-Wales. Llywelyn was caught with a small escort by an English patrol and killed; his head was struck off and sent to London, where it was paraded through the streets and displayed on the Tower. With Llywelyn dead, native Welsh resistance broke. His brother Dafydd ap Gruffudd was hunted down in summer 1283, betrayed and tried at Shrewsbury for treason. He was the first English nobleman ever sentenced to be hanged, drawn and quartered — the punishment Edward had devised for the rebellion.

The Statute of Rhuddlan, 1284

In March 1284 Edward issued the Statute of Rhuddlan, also known as the Statute of Wales. It dismantled the principality. The lands of Llywelyn became royal property. Gwynedd was divided into the new English-style counties of Anglesey, Caernarfon and Merioneth, with Cardigan and Carmarthen further south. Each had a sheriff, an exchequer and a system of writs and royal courts based on English common law — though some Welsh customs, such as partible inheritance, were tolerated. The Marcher lordships in eastern Wales kept their semi-independent status. The conquest had transformed political geography forever.

In autumn 1294 Madog ap Llywelyn led a large rebellion against the new English administration, taking advantage of Edward’s plans for a French campaign. Several castles were attacked and the unfinished works at Caernarfon were briefly captured and burned. Edward broke off his French expedition and crushed the rising in spring 1295. The lesson Edward drew was simple: the existing castle ring was not enough. He commissioned a final masterwork at Beaumaris on Anglesey to close the gap.

The Iron Ring of Castles

After the second war, Edward ordered the most ambitious castle programme in medieval Europe. Around the conquered north and west of Wales he built or rebuilt a chain of stone fortresses — later historians called this the ‘Iron Ring’. The four greatest were begun in 1283 and 1295: Conwy, Caernarfon, Harlech and Beaumaris. Each was placed where a fleet from England could resupply it by sea, so a Welsh rising could not starve the garrison. The total cost ran to roughly £80,000 across the programme — an enormous sum, equivalent to several years of royal income.

The architect of the programme was a Savoyard mason, Master James of St George. He brought ideas from the Alps: concentric walls (an outer ring inside an inner ring), polygonal towers and gatehouses that were small fortresses in their own right. Each castle was paired with a planned planted borough — a walled town settled with English merchants and craftsmen who paid rents directly to the king. Welsh inhabitants were excluded from these new towns by royal charter. The castles were instruments of military, political and economic control all at once.

Key Fact

The Iron Ring was a class of post-conquest fortifications — Conwy, Caernarfon, Harlech and Beaumaris — built or rebuilt after 1283 under Master James of St George. Each was sea-supplied, paired with a planted English borough and cost roughly £80,000 across the whole programme.

Costs and Consequences

The Welsh wars settled the political map of the British Isles for good. After 1284 Wales was no longer a separate principality. Edward’s eldest surviving son was created Prince of Wales in 1301 — the title English heirs to the throne have used ever since. The financial cost, however, was crushing. Castles, garrisons and campaign costs forced Edward into ever heavier taxation, including the wool tax of 1294, and into permanent dependence on Italian banking houses. When the Riccardi of Lucca collapsed under the strain in 1294, the king’s war chest collapsed with it — just as the Madog rising was starting.

Use precise dates and named individuals (Master James of St George, Madog ap Llywelyn) to anchor each step.

Key Takeaways

  • The first Welsh war (1277) ended with the Treaty of Aberconwy, reducing Llywelyn to a rump principality of Gwynedd; the second war (1282–83) ended with his death at Cilmeri and the execution of his brother Dafydd.
  • The Statute of Rhuddlan (1284) imposed English shire administration on conquered Gwynedd, dividing it into the new counties of Anglesey, Caernarfon and Merioneth.
  • The Iron Ring — Conwy, Caernarfon, Harlech and Beaumaris — was a class of sea-supplied fortifications, paired with planted boroughs, designed by Master James of St George at a total cost of around £80,000.

lessons.title: The Great Cause and the Conquest of Scotland, 1290-1296
lessons.description: The disputed Scottish succession, Balliol’s brief reign and the sack of Berwick.
lessons.content_html:
A Throne Without an Heir

In March 1286 the Scottish king Alexander III rode home through a stormy night to his new young queen at Kinghorn in Fife. His horse stumbled in the dark; he was thrown from a cliff and killed. With Alexander dead, all his children dead before him, Scotland was left without an adult heir. The throne passed to his three-year-old granddaughter, the ‘Maid of Norway’, Margaret — daughter of his daughter Margaret and Eric II of Norway. A council of six Scottish ‘Guardians’ took over the daily government and looked for a long-term solution.

Key Fact

The Scottish royal line collapsed in two stages. Alexander III died in March 1286 leaving no adult heir; his granddaughter Maid of Norway succeeded as queen of Scots but died aged seven in autumn 1290 on the voyage to Scotland, leaving thirteen rival candidates for the throne.

The Treaty of Birgham, 1290

In July 1290 the Treaty of Birgham agreed that the Maid of Norway would marry Edward I’s six-year-old heir, Edward of Caernarfon. The treaty insisted that Scotland would remain ‘separate and divided’ from England, with its own laws, courts and customs — the two kingdoms united only in the persons of the future king and queen. The arrangement promised a peaceful merger of the two crowns. Then came catastrophe. In late September 1290 the seven-year-old Maid sickened and died in Orkney before reaching the Scottish mainland. The proposed marriage was over; the throne stood vacant.

The Great Cause, 1291–92

Thirteen claimants came forward for the empty throne. The two strongest were John Balliol, Lord of Galloway, descended through the elder daughter of Earl David of Huntingdon, and Robert Bruce the Competitor (grandfather of the future Robert I), descended through the younger daughter but a generation closer. Civil war between their factions looked likely. The Guardians invited Edward I to arbitrate. Edward agreed — on the condition that the candidates first acknowledge him as overlord of Scotland.

In May 1291, on a meadow outside Norham on the English bank of the Tweed, the candidates and the Guardians swore that Edward was ‘Lord Paramount’ of Scotland. The hearings then opened. Over eighteen months — what Scottish writers later called the Great Cause — English and Scottish lawyers heard the rival claims. On 17 November 1292 Edward gave judgement at Berwick: the throne went to John Balliol. The decision was good law — primogeniture through the elder line — but the price was Scottish acceptance of an English overlord with a foot inside the kingdom.

Earlier English kings had received occasional acts of homage from Scottish rulers, but Edward took these scattered precedents and turned them into a doctrine. By forcing the candidates to accept his overlordship before they were heard, he locked the new king into a permanent legal relationship. The principle Edward applied was simple: a king of Scots who held his crown by Edward’s judgement could be summoned to English courts, asked for military service, and overruled in his own kingdom. This is what set Scottish nobles against him within four years.

Balliol’s Brief Reign, 1292–96

John Balliol was crowned at Scone on 30 November 1292. His reign lasted barely three years and was disastrous. Edward repeatedly humiliated him — allowing Scottish appellants to bring lawsuits against the king of Scots in the English court at Westminster, treating Balliol as just another vassal. In 1294 Edward summoned Balliol with a feudal demand for Scottish troops to fight in his French war. The Scottish nobles refused. In July 1295 they appointed a council of twelve to govern in Balliol’s name and signed the auld alliance with Philip IV of France — the first formal treaty between Scotland and France. From an English perspective this was open rebellion.

The Sack of Berwick, March 1296

Edward responded with overwhelming force. In late March 1296 his army crossed the Tweed and besieged Berwick-upon-Tweed, then Scotland’s richest port and a major centre of Flemish trade. The town’s defences were poor and on 30 March Edward stormed it. What followed was a deliberate massacre. English chroniclers admitted that the slaughter went on for two days; some Scottish accounts put the dead at 7,000 men, women and children. The Flemish merchants of the Red Hall fought to the last and were burned alive when the building collapsed. Berwick’s prosperity was destroyed; the town would never again be the trading capital of Scotland.

Dunbar and the Deposition of Balliol

A Scottish army moved to relieve the border. On 27 April 1296 Edward’s cavalry crushed it at the Battle of Dunbar; the Scottish leadership surrendered en masse. Edward marched north almost without resistance. At Montrose on 8 July 1296 he ritually stripped Balliol of his royal regalia — the empty surcoat earned him the nickname Toom Tabard, ‘empty coat’. Balliol was sent to the Tower of London. Edward took the great seal of Scotland, broke it into four pieces, and sent the symbols of Scottish kingship south — including the Stone of Scone, the ancient inauguration stone of Scottish kings.

By August 1296 Edward had returned south claiming Scotland as a conquered territory. He left an English administration in place under John Warenne, Earl of Surrey. To Edward, the kingdom of Scotland had ceased to exist; it was now simply a province of his realm. To Scots, he had carried out a hostile occupation. The seeds of the long war had been sown.

Edward placed the Stone of Scone beneath a special oak chair, the Coronation Chair, in Westminster Abbey. Every English monarch since Edward II has been crowned over it. The stone became one of the most loaded political objects in British history: stolen briefly by Scottish nationalists in 1950 and finally returned to Scotland in 1996, seven hundred years after Edward had taken it. It is an exact measure of how powerful a symbol Edward had captured.

Key Fact

The Great Cause (1291–92) made Edward I overlord of Scotland and chose John Balliol as king. Balliol’s 1295 alliance with France triggered Edward’s invasion of 1296: the sack of Berwick (30 March), the victory at Dunbar (27 April), and the public deposition of ‘Toom Tabard’ at Montrose (8 July) ended the Scottish kingdom for the moment.

Show how Alexander III’s sudden death in 1286 led to the Maid of Norway’s death in 1290, which led to the Great Cause and Edward’s overlordship in 1291–92, which led to Balliol’s humiliation, which led to the auld alliance in 1295, which led to the invasion of 1296. Use precise dates and named places (Norham, Berwick, Dunbar, Montrose, Scone) to anchor each step.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The deaths of Alexander III (1286) and the Maid of Norway (1290) left Scotland without an adult heir; the Great Cause of 1291–92 made Edward I the arbiter and recognised him as ‘Lord Paramount’ of Scotland.
  • John Balliol was chosen king in November 1292 but humiliated repeatedly by Edward; in 1295 his council of twelve signed the ‘auld alliance’ with France, the first formal Scottish–French treaty.
  • The 1296 invasion saw the sack of Berwick, the victory at Dunbar, the deposition of ‘Toom Tabard’ at Montrose and the seizure of the Stone of Scone — placed in Westminster Abbey until 1996.

• The 1294 demand for Scottish troops to fight in France caused the appointment of a council of twelve and the auld alliance of 1295, the first Scottish–French treaty.
• The deteriorating relationship caused Edward’s invasion in 1296, the sack of Berwick and the deposition of Balliol — ending the kingdom of Scotland in Edward’s eyes.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the sack of Berwick (March 1296) for the war between England and Scotland.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Berwick was Scotland’s richest port and a major centre of Flemish trade; its destruction wiped out a key economic base of the Scottish crown.
• The two-day massacre with up to 7,000 dead, including the Flemish merchants of the Red Hall, made the war unmistakeably one of conquest and not mere arbitration.
• It cleared the way for Dunbar (April) and the deposition of Balliol at Montrose (July), allowing Edward to claim Scotland as a conquered territory by August 1296.
• Significance over time: Berwick never again recovered its position as the trading capital of Scotland, and the memory of the sack hardened Scottish resistance through the rest of Edward’s reign.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using examples from the period 1286–1296, that John Balliol’s humiliation was the main reason for the war between England and Scotland.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Edward repeatedly allowed Scottish appellants to bring lawsuits against Balliol in the English court at Westminster, treating the king of Scots as a vassal.
• The 1294 feudal demand that Balliol provide troops for the French war was deliberately humiliating and impossible to obey.
• Scottish nobles set up a council of twelve in 1295 to govern in Balliol’s name precisely because they thought he could no longer act as a free king.
• The auld alliance of 1295 was the direct response to that humiliation and provoked Edward’s 1296 invasion.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Edward’s overlordship had been built into the Great Cause from 1291 — the legal trap was set before Balliol was chosen.
• The dynastic accident of Alexander III’s 1286 death and the Maid of Norway’s 1290 death created the vacuum into which Edward stepped.
• Edward’s wider strategy of pressing English overlordship across the British Isles — already shown in Wales — would have produced conflict with Scotland eventually whoever was king.
• The economic strain of war with France in 1294 — the maltolt, the Riccardi collapse — made conquest of Scotland the cheapest source of additional revenue.

A strong response weighs Balliol’s personal humiliation against the deeper structural pressures and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

[16 marks]

Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on multiple factors and a supported judgement.
Developing: Description of more than one factor with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described with no real judgement.

lessons.title: Wallace, Bruce and the 'Hammer of the Scots', 1297-1307
lessons.description: Scottish resistance, the First War of Scottish Independence and Edward I’s contested legacy.
lessons.content_html:
A Conquered Kingdom That Would Not Stay Conquered

In August 1296, when Edward I rode south claiming Scotland as a conquered territory, he believed the war was over. Within twelve months it was clear it had only begun. The English administration left under John Warenne, Earl of Surrey, was harsh and unpopular: Scottish lords were forced to swear loyalty to Edward in person on the ‘Ragman Roll’, English officials taxed Scottish trade for the king’s war chest, and an attempt to conscript Scottish men into the French campaign provoked outrage. By spring 1297 risings broke out in the south-west and the north. Two figures emerged to lead them — a young knight from Renfrewshire called William Wallace, and a Highland nobleman called Andrew Murray.

Key Fact

Four pivotal battles shaped the First War of Scottish Independence under Edward I: Stirling Bridge (September 1297, Scottish victory), Falkirk (July 1298, English victory), the campaign of 1303–04 ending in Edward’s acceptance of Scottish surrender at Strathord, and Methven (June 1306, defeat of the newly crowned Robert Bruce).

William Wallace and Stirling Bridge, 1297

William Wallace was an obscure younger son of a Scottish knight; he killed an English sheriff at Lanark in May 1297, sparking a wider rising in the lowlands. Andrew Murray simultaneously raised the north. By September their armies had joined and were waiting at Stirling, the gateway between northern and southern Scotland. On 11 September 1297 Surrey’s English army began crossing the narrow wooden bridge over the River Forth two abreast. When roughly half the army was over, Wallace and Murray charged. The English vanguard was cut to pieces, the bridge collapsed under the panicked retreat and as many as 5,000 English soldiers were killed or drowned. Murray died of his wounds soon after, leaving Wallace alone in command. He was knighted and named ‘Guardian of Scotland’ in March 1298.

Falkirk and the Rise of the Longbow, 1298

Edward returned in person and met Wallace’s army outside Falkirk on 22 July 1298. Wallace deployed his spearmen in four schiltrons — tight circles of spearmen with their points levelled outwards in every direction. The schiltrons broke the first English cavalry charges easily. Then Edward called up his Welsh and Cheshire longbowmen, who poured arrows into the static formations until the schiltrons crumbled. The cavalry then charged the survivors. Wallace escaped but his army was destroyed.

Falkirk marked the emergence of the longbow as the dominant English battlefield weapon. Edward had recruited massed archers from the Welsh borders during the conquest of Wales, and now he turned them on the Scots. The combination of disciplined spearmen broken by archery and finished by cavalry would shape English warfare for the next 150 years — through Crécy (1346) and Agincourt (1415).

After Falkirk Wallace resigned the Guardianship and waged a guerrilla campaign for seven years, travelling to France to seek support from Philip IV. He was finally betrayed in August 1305 near Glasgow by John de Menteith, a Scottish knight loyal to Edward, and brought to London. He was tried in Westminster Hall on 23 August 1305 with a crown of laurels on his head — mocking his refusal to acknowledge Edward as king of Scotland. He was hanged, drawn and quartered the same day, his head set on a pike on London Bridge, his quarters sent to Newcastle, Berwick, Stirling and Perth. The brutality made Wallace a Scottish national martyr at the moment Edward intended to erase him.

Robert Bruce’s Coup and Coronation, 1306

In February 1306 the war broke open again. Robert Bruce, Earl of Carrick — grandson of the Bruce who had been a Competitor for the throne in 1291 — met John Comyn, his rival for leadership of Scottish resistance, in the Greyfriars church at Dumfries. The argument turned violent. Bruce stabbed Comyn at the high altar and rode out to seize the throne. On 25 March 1306 Bruce was crowned at Scone — without the captured Stone, but with a new circlet borrowed from the regalia.

Edward responded with cold fury. He extended the punishment of treason to families: Bruce’s sister Mary and the Countess of Buchan, who had crowned him, were hung in iron cages outside Roxburgh and Berwick castles. Three of Bruce’s brothers were hanged, drawn and quartered. The new English commander, Aymer de Valence, defeated Bruce at the Battle of Methven on 19 June 1306; the king of Scots fled into the Highlands and the western islands. By autumn 1306 he was a hunted fugitive.

Edward’s Death at Burgh-by-Sands, 1307

In May 1307 Bruce returned to Ayrshire and won small but symbolic engagements at Glentrool and Loudoun Hill. Edward, now nearly seventy and seriously ill, had himself carried north on a litter to renew the campaign in person. On 7 July 1307 he died at Burgh-by-Sands on the south shore of the Solway Firth, just inside the English border. His body was returned to Westminster and buried in a plain marble tomb. His son, the new Edward II, abandoned the campaign and turned south.

Historians divide on the legacy. Marc Morris portrays Edward as a ‘great and terrible king’ who shaped Britain by the sword and the gallows; the Scottish writer Fiona Watson stresses that Edward’s war ultimately welded Scotland into a fierce national consciousness against him. Michael Prestwich emphasises Edward’s administrative achievements at home, arguing that the Scottish failure should not erase the rest of the reign. The contested label on the tomb captures all three views — an English Crown commemorating victory while admitting, by adding the inscription long after the event, that the title needed defending.

The ‘Hammer of the Scots’

The famous title Hammer of the Scots — in Latin, Scottorum Malleus — was not Edward’s contemporary nickname. It was inscribed on his tomb at Westminster Abbey long after his death, possibly as late as the sixteenth century. The reality at his death was very different. Robert Bruce was a crowned king of Scots, raising new armies in the Highlands. Wallace had been turned into a martyr. The 1296 conquest had not held. Edward’s son inherited a Scottish war he could not win, and within seven years of Edward’s death the Scots would crush an English army at Bannockburn (1314) under Edward II.

Key Fact

The ‘Hammer of the Scots’ (Scottorum Malleus) is a tomb inscription at Westminster Abbey, added long after Edward’s death and probably as late as the sixteenth century. It was not a contemporary nickname — at his death in July 1307 Robert Bruce was an anointed king of Scots and the Scottish war was very much unfinished.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 16-mark Period Argument question on Edward I’s reputation, the highest band rewards a substantiated overall judgement — not just balanced description. Use the ‘Hammer of the Scots’ misconception to your advantage: examiners reward students who recognise the label as a later tomb inscription rather than a contemporary verdict. Weigh the brutal punishments and the unfinished conquest against the genuine military victories at Falkirk and Methven, and reach a clear judgement of your own. Use precise dates (Stirling Bridge 11 September 1297, Falkirk 22 July 1298, Methven 19 June 1306, Burgh-by-Sands 7 July 1307).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • William Wallace and Andrew Murray crushed Surrey’s army at Stirling Bridge (1297); Edward’s longbowmen broke the schiltrons at Falkirk (1298); Wallace was captured and executed in 1305.
  • Robert Bruce killed his rival Comyn at the Greyfriars in Dumfries in February 1306, was crowned at Scone in March, defeated at Methven in June, but renewed his campaign in 1307.
  • Edward I died at Burgh-by-Sands on 7 July 1307 with Scotland still defiant; the ‘Hammer of the Scots’ (Scottorum Malleus) tomb inscription is a posthumous label, not a contemporary verdict.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Battle of Falkirk (1298) on the Anglo-Scottish war.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The destruction of the schiltrons by massed Welsh and Cheshire longbowmen caused the longbow to emerge as Edward’s decisive battlefield weapon.
• Wallace’s defeat caused him to resign the Guardianship and turn to a guerrilla campaign and diplomatic work in France.
• Falkirk caused a tactical lesson that shaped English warfare for 150 years — armoured cavalry combined with massed archers, used at Crécy and Agincourt.
• The battle did not end Scottish resistance — instead it caused a longer war of small engagements and changing leadership, leaving Scotland unconquered when Edward died.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Multiple effects developed with precise figures and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Two or more effects explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of William Wallace for the First War of Scottish Independence.

• His public title of ‘Guardian of Scotland’ gave Scottish resistance a legitimate political voice between 1297 and 1298.
• His brutal execution in August 1305 — tried with a laurel crown, hanged, drawn and quartered — turned him into a Scottish national martyr at the moment Edward intended to erase him.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Edward I’s death at Burgh-by-Sands (1307) for the Anglo-Scottish war.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Edward had been carried north on a litter to lead the renewed war in person; his death on 7 July 1307 left the campaign without its most committed leader.
• His son and heir, Edward II, abandoned the march and turned south — giving Robert Bruce the breathing room he needed to rebuild a Scottish army.
• The 1296 conquest was now visibly unfinished: an anointed king of Scots in arms, no decisive English presence north of the Forth.
• Significance over time: within seven years of Edward’s death the Scots crushed Edward II’s army at Bannockburn (1314), and the ‘Hammer of the Scots’ tomb inscription was added long afterwards as the verdict it had failed to earn in life.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using examples from across the period 1296–1307, how far Edward I deserves the title ‘Hammer of the Scots’.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support of the title:
• Edward stormed and sacked Berwick in 1296 with thousands of dead and crushed the Scottish army at Dunbar within a month, deposing John Balliol the same year.
• At Falkirk in 1298 he destroyed Wallace’s schiltrons with massed longbow fire, breaking organised Scottish resistance for years.
• His commander Aymer de Valence defeated Robert Bruce at Methven (1306), forcing Bruce into hiding.
• His punishments — hanging Bruce’s brothers, caging the women who crowned him, executing Wallace as a traitor — were brutal expressions of royal power.

Arguments against the title:
• The label is a tomb inscription added long after Edward’s death, possibly in the sixteenth century, not a contemporary verdict.
• At his death in July 1307 Robert Bruce was an anointed king of Scots raising armies in the Highlands.
• The brutality at Berwick, Wallace’s execution and the caging of Bruce’s female allies created the very martyrs that fuelled the Scottish cause.
• Within seven years of Edward’s death his son was crushed at Bannockburn (1314); the ‘hammering’ clearly did not stick.

A strong response weighs the genuine victories against the unfinished nature of the conquest and reaches a substantiated overall judgement — for example, that Edward earned the title in his own court but not from history.

[16 marks]
Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides and a supported judgement.
Developing: Description of more than one factor with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described with no real judgement.

lessons.title: The Battle of Stirling Bridge: Historic Environment 2027
lessons.description: The 2027 specified site. A bridge two horsemen wide, a loop of soft ground, and the day Edward's cavalry counted for nothing.
lessons.content_html:
Why This Site Matters

The Battle of Stirling Bridge is your specified site for the 2027 exam. The 16-mark question on Paper 2 will name it, and it will reward one thing above all: showing how the place — a narrow bridge, a river loop, soft meadow and a crag — turned the finest heavy cavalry in Britain into casualties. Lessons 10 and 11 give you the story of Edward and Scotland; this lesson walks the ground of 11 September 1297.

How Edward's Scotland Caught Fire

In 1296 Edward I had crushed Scotland in a single campaign: Berwick sacked, the Scots army beaten at Dunbar, King John Balliol stripped of his crown, and English officials installed to run the country. Chief among them was Hugh de Cressingham, Edward’s treasurer, whose taxes made him the most hated man in Scotland. By the summer of 1297 revolt had broken out in two places at once — William Wallace in the south-west, Andrew Moray in the north-east. Their combined force met the English army at the one place every army marching north had to pass: Stirling.

Key Fact

Stirling was called the gateway to the Highlands: its castle guarded the lowest crossing of the River Forth. An army moving between southern and northern Scotland had little practical choice but to cross here — which is why the battle happened where it did.

Reading the Ground: Bridge, Loop and Crag

The site has three features you must be able to describe. First, the bridge itself: a narrow wooden crossing over the Forth, so tight — chroniclers say — that only two horsemen could ride abreast. An army of thousands could only trickle across it. Second, the ground beyond the bridge: the crossing led onto a low carse inside a tight loop of the river — soft, wet meadow threaded by a single raised causeway, with water curling round it on three sides. Third, Abbey Craig: a steep volcanic crag a mile north of the bridge, where the Wallace Monument stands today. From its slopes Wallace and Moray could watch the entire English crossing while their own men stayed hidden and rested.

Put the three together and the trap describes itself. Whatever crossed the bridge would be stuck on soft ground in a river loop, with no room to form up, no firm footing for a cavalry charge, and an enemy waiting on high ground above the only exit.

The Armies and the Commanders

The English army was commanded by John de Warenne, Earl of Surrey, the victor of Dunbar — elderly, unwell and openly reluctant to be in Scotland at all — with Cressingham at his side urging speed and economy. Their force was built around armoured knights, supported by thousands of infantry including Welsh spearmen. The Scots had no comparable cavalry and no great lords present: Wallace and Moray led spearmen — ordinary freemen with twelve-foot spears — positioned on and behind Abbey Craig. On paper it was no contest. On that ground, the paper was wrong.

Chroniclers record that a Scottish knight in English service, Sir Richard Lundie, warned the council that the bridge was a death-trap and offered to lead a mounted force across a ford upstream, where sixty horsemen could cross at once, to take the Scots in the flank. Cressingham objected that a delay would waste the king’s money, and Warenne ordered the direct crossing. The site question rewards you for knowing this: the English saw the danger of the ground and chose it anyway.

The Battle: A Trap Sprung at Half-Time

Early on 11 September 1297 the English began filing across the bridge two abreast — a crossing so slow that chroniclers claim it had already been started and recalled more than once, with Warenne at one point oversleeping while his vanguard stood on the wrong bank. Wallace and Moray watched from Abbey Craig and did nothing. They let perhaps half the English army — the vanguard of knights and infantry, Cressingham among them — assemble on the soft ground inside the loop.

Then the spearmen charged down from the crag. Their first target was not the vanguard but the bridgehead itself: seize the end of the bridge, and the army was cut in two. It worked. The knights inside the loop turned to charge and found their warhorses floundering in the carse; the causeway could hold no formation; and the river hemmed them in on three sides. Some fought and died where they stood, some drowned trying to swim the Forth in armour, one knight famously hacked his way back across the bridge. Warenne, watching from the south bank with half an army, could feed no help through a two-horse-wide bottleneck into a collapsing pocket. He ordered the bridge destroyed and retreated to Berwick.

Key Fact

The bridge that fed the English army into the trap also stopped its rescue. Once the Scots held the northern bridgehead, the width of the bridge — two horsemen abreast — meant Warenne’s remaining thousands might as well have been in England.

The Cost and the Aftermath

Chroniclers put the English dead in the thousands, including around a hundred knights — staggering losses for the class of men who were rarely killed in battle, because ransoming them was profitable. Spearmen on foot took no ransoms. Cressingham was killed and, the chronicles record with relish, flayed — pieces of his skin kept as trophies, one allegedly made into a belt for Wallace’s sword. The victory made Wallace Guardian of Scotland and shattered the assumption that knights simply beat infantry. But it came at a price: Andrew Moray, the rising's ablest soldier, was mortally wounded and died within months. And it guaranteed the return of Edward himself, who took personal command and destroyed Wallace’s army in the open field at Falkirk the following summer — flat, firm ground, no bridge, no loop — which is the sharpest possible proof of what the Stirling site had been worth.

The Site Today and in the Exam

The wooden bridge is gone — a later stone bridge stands close to the spot — but the loop of the Forth, the carse and Abbey Craig, now crowned by the Victorian Wallace Monument, still let you read the battle from the ground. In the 16-mark question, work feature by feature: the bridge as bottleneck explains why only half the army fought; the carse explains why cavalry was useless; the loop explains why there was no escape; Abbey Craig explains why the Scots could choose the perfect moment; and Stirling’s position as the gateway crossing explains why the battle happened here at all. Feature, consequence, link to the statement — every time.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The examiner rewards precision about ground, not adjectives. ‘The battlefield was boggy’ is weak. ‘The crossing led onto soft carse inside a loop of the Forth, so the vanguard’s warhorses could neither charge nor withdraw once the Scots held the bridgehead’ ties a named feature to a named consequence — that is site knowledge earning Level 4, not scene-setting.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The battle happened at Stirling because geography made it the gateway to northern Scotland: the castle guarded the lowest practical crossing of the Forth.
  • Three site features decided it: a bridge two horsemen wide, soft carse inside a river loop, and Abbey Craig giving the Scots observation and the choice of moment.
  • Wallace and Moray sprang the trap at half-time: seizing the bridgehead cut the English army in two and left knights floundering on ground that cancelled cavalry.
  • The consequences ran both ways — Wallace became Guardian and the myth of knightly invincibility died, but Moray was mortally wounded, and Falkirk in 1298 showed the same Scots army destroyed on ground that gave it no protection.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the battlefield site at Stirling Bridge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The wooden bridge: so narrow that only two horsemen could cross abreast, it fed the English army across the Forth at a trickle and could not pass reinforcements once the fighting began.
• The carse: soft, wet meadow inside a tight loop of the river, crossed by a single causeway — ground on which armoured cavalry could not charge or manoeuvre.
• Abbey Craig: the steep crag a mile north of the crossing from which Wallace and Moray observed the crossing and timed their attack.
• The river loop: the Forth curled round the low ground on three sides, leaving troops caught there no way out except the bridge.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the English army that fought at Stirling Bridge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Its core was armoured knights on warhorses — the arm that had won at Dunbar in 1296 but was cancelled by the soft carse.
• It was commanded by John de Warenne, Earl of Surrey, elderly and reluctant, with the treasurer Hugh de Cressingham pressing for speed and economy.
• It substantially outnumbered the Scots and included thousands of infantry, including Welsh spearmen — but only the portion across the bridge could fight.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the site of Stirling Bridge for the outcome of the battle.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The bridge as bottleneck: only part of the army could cross before the attack, so the Scots fought half the English force with all of their own.
• The bridgehead seizure: once the Scots held the northern end, the remaining English strength was irrelevant — the width of the bridge stopped any rescue.
• The carse and loop: soft ground cancelled the English advantage in heavy cavalry and the river cut off retreat, turning defeat into destruction.
• Comparison strengthens the point: at Falkirk in 1298, on firm open ground, the same Scots army was destroyed — the site was the difference.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the Battle of Stirling Bridge, 11 September 1297.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The approach: Wallace and Moray positioned on Abbey Craig; the English under Warenne and Cressingham at the bridge; Lundie's warning about a ford ignored on grounds of cost.
• The crossing: the army files over two abreast through the morning; the Scots wait until roughly half — vanguard, knights, Cressingham — is inside the river loop.
• The attack: spearmen charge from the crag and seize the bridgehead; knights flounder on the carse; some drown in the Forth; Cressingham is killed.
• The end: Warenne, unable to reinforce across the bottleneck, destroys the bridge and retreats to Berwick; thousands of English dead including around a hundred knights.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Battle of Stirling Bridge on Edward I's rule of Scotland.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• English administration collapsed: the hated treasurer Cressingham was dead, Warenne retreated to Berwick, and Scotland north of the border was effectively lost for a season.
• Wallace's rise: the victory made him Guardian of Scotland and gave the revolt a leader with proven success, followed by raids into northern England.
• Edward's response: the defeat brought the king back to take personal command, leading to Falkirk in 1298 and the far longer, costlier wars that followed.
• Military lesson: the battle punctured the assumption that mounted knights automatically beat infantry — though Falkirk showed the lesson was about ground, not spearmen alone.

practice_questions.text: 'The English lost at Stirling Bridge because of their commanders' mistakes rather than the strength of the Scots' position.' How far does a study of the site of the Battle of Stirling Bridge support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to the site and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• The English council knew the ground: Lundie warned that the bridge was a trap and offered a flanking crossing by the ford; Cressingham's concern for cost and Warenne's lethargy sent the army over anyway.
• The shambolic crossing — started, recalled, restarted, with Warenne reportedly oversleeping — handed the Scots their timing.
Against the statement (site evidence):
• The position would have punished even competent handling: any force beyond the bridge stood on carse inside a river loop, and no commander could widen a two-horse bridge under attack.
• Wallace and Moray used the site with real skill — waiting on Abbey Craig, letting half the army cross, then striking the bridgehead rather than the vanguard.
• Context: Stirling was the unavoidable gateway crossing, so the English had limited strategic choice about meeting the enemy there.
A developed judgement weighing commander error against the inherent strength of the site is required for the top level.

lessons.title: Acton Burnell Castle: Historic Environment 2028
lessons.description: The 2028 specified site. A chancellor's red sandstone house with big windows — and why 'castle' is the least accurate word for it.
lessons.content_html:
The Castle That Isn't One

Acton Burnell Castle is your specified site for the 2028 exam, and the first thing to understand is that its name misleads. This is not a fortress like the great castles Edward built in Wales (Lesson 9). It is a fortified manor house in rural Shropshire — a rich man’s residence wearing a light costume of battlements — and that is exactly why AQA chose it. The building shows you Edward’s England from an unexpected angle: what power, wealth and royal favour looked like at home, in peacetime, in the reign of a king you have mostly met at war.

The Man Behind the House

The house was built by Robert Burnell, the most powerful royal servant of the age. A Shropshire clerk who rose in Edward’s service before the king came to the throne, Burnell became Chancellor of England in 1274 and Bishop of Bath and Wells in 1275, and he held the chancellorship until his death in 1292 — nearly the whole working reign. Wherever Edward was, government ran through Burnell. He was also spectacularly rich, holding dozens of manors, and in the 1280s he set about rebuilding the village he was born in: a grand house for himself, a fine parish church beside it, at the family manor of Acton Burnell.

Key Fact

Robert Burnell — Chancellor of England from 1274 and Bishop of Bath and Wells from 1275 — began his grand house around the time of the 1284 licence, with work continuing to his death in 1292. In January 1284 Edward granted him a licence to crenellate: royal permission to add battlements.

Reading the Building: Comfort Wearing Armour

Walk round the roofless red sandstone shell today and the domestic truth shows through the military dress. The building is a compact rectangular block with a tower at each corner — castle-shaped at first glance. But look closer, as the examiner wants you to. The windows are large, elegant and low enough to climb through; a real fortress has arrow slits. There is no moat, no curtain wall of any strength, no gatehouse, no room for a garrison. Inside, the block held a first-floor great hall with private chambers — a design for entertaining, administration and comfortable living. The battlements are real, but they are jewellery. This is what historians call a fortified manor house, with the emphasis firmly on manor house.

The licence to crenellate completes the point. By Edward’s reign such licences were largely honours — the architectural equivalent of a knighthood. A licence said publicly: this man matters to the king. Burnell’s house did not need battlements to survive Shropshire; it needed them to be seen.

The Parliament in the Barn

Acton Burnell earned its place in national history in the autumn of 1283, when Edward — in the Marches for the aftermath of the second Welsh war — held a parliament at Burnell’s manor. Tradition places its sessions in the great barn whose two massive gable ends still stand near the house. From that assembly came the Statute of Acton Burnell, a law that let merchants register debts and recover them quickly through the courts. It seems a dry subject until you see what it shows: Edward legislating for traders and credit, parliament meeting wherever the king happened to be — including at the private house of his chief minister — and the reach of royal law-making extending into everyday commercial life, the theme you met in Lesson 3.

Edward’s wars ran on credit, much of it from Italian merchant-bankers (Lesson 4). Merchants would only lend and trade freely in a kingdom where debts could actually be collected, so the statute made at Acton Burnell in 1283 — strengthened two years later at Westminster — was war finance by other means. The site links the barn in Shropshire to the wool trade, the Riccardi bankers and the conquest of Wales in one chain of evidence.

What the Site Shows About Edward's England

Set Acton Burnell beside Caernarfon (Lesson 9) and the pair explain the reign. In conquered Wales, Edward built true war castles — concentric walls, garrisons, fortress-towns. In the English Midlands, his chancellor built a house with big windows and ornamental battlements. The same king, the same decade, opposite buildings — because England itself was at peace, governed by law, taxes and parliaments rather than by garrisons. The house also shows the rise of a new kind of power: Burnell was neither a great baron nor a warrior, but a professional administrator raised by royal service to wealth that built in stone. And the parliament of 1283 shows government travelling with the king, making national law for commerce from a Shropshire manor.

Key Fact

Acton Burnell and Caernarfon rose in the same decade for the same king’s regime — a comfortable lightly-fortified house in a peaceful England, a war fortress in a conquered Wales. The contrast is the single most useful idea in your site answer.

The Site Afterwards and in the Exam

Burnell died in 1292; his family's fortunes faded within a couple of generations; the house was abandoned by the early fifteenth century and has long stood a roofless shell, preserved as a romantic ruin. The red sandstone walls, corner towers, window openings and the barn’s gable ends survive in English Heritage care, free to visit. In the 16-mark question, read features as evidence: large windows and thin defences → peace and comfort; the licence to crenellate → status culture around royal favour; the barn parliament and statute → law-making, credit and the reach of royal government; the builder’s career → the administrator’s rise. Feature, meaning, link to the statement — every paragraph.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The trap in this site is describing it as a castle and reciting siege features it does not have. The marks live in the mismatch: name a domestic feature (great windows, first-floor hall, no gatehouse), name the military costume (battlements under a status licence), and say what the combination proves about Edward’s England — a governed, peaceful realm where display had replaced defence.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Acton Burnell is a fortified manor house of the 1280s, built in red sandstone by Robert Burnell — Chancellor from 1274, Bishop of Bath and Wells from 1275, Edward's indispensable minister until 1292.
  • Its features argue peace: great windows, a first-floor hall and corner towers with ornamental battlements, licensed by the king in 1284 as a mark of favour rather than a preparation for war.
  • The 1283 parliament at the manor — traditionally in the barn whose gable ends still stand — produced the Statute of Acton Burnell, speeding debt recovery for merchants and tying the site to trade, credit and royal law-making.
  • Read against Caernarfon, the site completes the picture of the reign: war castles for conquered Wales, comfortable houses and parliaments for a governed England.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Acton Burnell Castle.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A compact rectangular red sandstone block with a tower at each corner and battlements licensed in 1284 — castle costume on a house.
• Large, elegant windows set low in the walls, where a real fortress would have arrow slits.
• A first-floor great hall with private chambers, designed for administration, entertaining and comfort.
• No moat, strong curtain wall, gatehouse or garrison accommodation.
• The great barn nearby, whose surviving gable ends mark the traditional meeting place of the 1283 parliament.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Robert Burnell's career that explain the house he built.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Chancellor of England from 1274 until his death in 1292 — head of Edward's administration for nearly the whole working reign.
• Bishop of Bath and Wells from 1275 — church office and income stacked on state office.
• Enormous landed wealth accumulated through royal service, funding building at his birthplace village.
• A professional administrator rather than a warrior baron — the new kind of power the house embodies.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the licence to crenellate granted for Acton Burnell in 1284.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It shows fortification as status: by the 1280s a licence advertised royal favour more than military need, and Burnell's battlements were ornament on a domestic house.
• It shows royal control: even the appearance of fortification in England required the king's permission — a contrast with the anarchy of private castles in earlier reigns.
• Its timing shows the reward culture around Edward's servants: granted at the height of Burnell's indispensability, alongside the parliament held at his manor.
• It supports the site's biggest argument: England at peace, where defence had become display.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the parliament held at Acton Burnell in 1283 and what came of it.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Context: autumn 1283, Edward in the Welsh Marches following the second Welsh war and the fall of Dafydd; government travelling with the king.
• The setting: parliament summoned to the Shropshire manor of the Chancellor, Robert Burnell; tradition places the sessions in the great barn whose gable ends survive.
• The outcome: the Statute of Acton Burnell, letting merchants register debts before mayors and recover them quickly, strengthened by the Statute of Merchants at Westminster in 1285.
• The meaning: royal law reaching into commercial life, credit protected because Edward's wars ran on it, and a private house hosting national government.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Acton Burnell as evidence about government in Edward I's England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The rise of the administrator: the house was built not by birth or conquest but by office — Burnell's chancellorship turned service into stone.
• Government on the move: a parliament at a minister's rural manor shows royal government operating wherever the king stood.
• Law for commerce: the 1283 statute connects the site to wool, credit and the Italian bankers financing Edward's wars.
• Peace as the precondition: a chief minister could build for comfort in the Midlands because royal justice, not private war, ruled England.

practice_questions.text: 'Acton Burnell shows that castles were no longer needed in Edward I's England.' How far does a study of Acton Burnell support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to Acton Burnell and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• The building itself: great windows, first-floor hall, no serious defences — a house in castle costume, safe in a governed shire.
• The licence to crenellate as honour rather than necessity shows fortification reduced to heraldry in England.
• The barn parliament and debt statute show a realm ruled by law, parliaments and credit — the tools that had replaced garrisons.
Against the statement (contextual knowledge):
• The same regime was simultaneously building Caernarfon, Conwy and Harlech — where rule was contested, true castles were still indispensable.
• Within twenty years, Scottish war would show fortresses deciding campaigns (Lessons 10-11).
• So the accurate judgement is geographical: castles were no longer needed in the pacified English heartland, and precisely because royal power there rested on the law and finance the site itself commemorates.
A developed judgement distinguishing England from the reign's frontiers is required for the top level.

glossary_terms.definition: The king's chief minister, keeper of the great seal, head of the royal writing office and effectively the head of government administration.
Royal permission to fortify a building with battlements; by Edward I's reign often granted as a mark of status rather than for real military need.
A comfortable residence dressed with light fortifications such as battlements and corner towers, built for status rather than serious defence.
The 1283 law, made at the parliament held at Acton Burnell, giving merchants a fast legal process to recover debts registered before mayors.
The border region between England and Wales, where royal and baronial power met and Edward's Welsh wars were organised.
